#### Q26: Sketch the graph of an influenza epidemic (cases vs. time)

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — declare which curve you are sketching</b></summary>

Cover everything below. First decision, stated aloud: **cumulative cases** (S-shaped, saturating) or **daily new cases** (bell-shaped, one peak)? The two are derivative and integral of each other, and conflating them is the question's first trap. Pick daily new cases for the dramatic sketch — then state that its integral is the cumulative S-curve.

> "Sketch an epidemic" is under-specified on purpose. Naming your variable and its units before drawing is the modelling behaviour being tested.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "Why does the curve rise, turn, and fall? Give the mechanism in one sentence."</b></summary>

Formulate the mechanism yourself before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

The SIR picture: each infection converts a Susceptible to Infected (at rate β·S·I) and each infection recovers (at rate γ·I). The bell curve is dI/dt = βSI/N − γI = I(βS/N − γ): while susceptibles are plentiful the bracket is positive and growth is exponential; the bracket shrinks as S falls; the curve peaks when the bracket hits zero, i.e. S = Nγ/β = N/R₀; afterwards there are too few susceptibles to sustain transmission and the curve decays.

One equation, three phases: exponential rise, peak at S = N/R₀, burnout decline.

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: The cumulative curve and its numbers</b></summary>

The cumulative count C(t) follows the logistic law

C(t) = (K)/(1 + e^(−r(t−t₀)))

- K = final attack size (total ever infected); r sets the initial exponential growth rate; t₀ is the inflection point — where C′ peaks, at C = K/2 for the symmetric logistic.
- **Herd immunity threshold**: if vaccination (or prior infection) immunises a fraction f with f > 1 − 1/R₀, the epidemic cannot take off — R₀(1−f) ⋖ 1. Numbers: flu R₀ ≈ 1.3 → threshold ≈ 23%; a COVID-like R₀ ≈ 3 → ≈ 67%; measles R₀ ≈ 12–18 → ≈ 92%. Higher R₀, harsher the vaccination bar.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — the annotated sketch</b></summary>

Daily-cases bell: near-zero tail during incubation; exponential rise (log-linear early phase); single asymmetric peak (the decline is usually *slower* than the rise — depletion of susceptibles is gradual, and interventions asymmetric); long right tail decaying to zero. Cumulative S-curve underneath: inflection under the peak, saturating at K. Labels: axes (time, cases/day), peak height ∝ R₀-dependent transmissibility, area under the bell = K.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **Cumulative vs. incidence**: the S-curve and the bell are not two candidate answers — they are integral and derivative. Say which you sketch and how the other follows.
2. **Symmetric bell assumption**: real epidemic curves are typically right-skewed (slow burnout; superspreading; staged interventions). A symmetric Gaussian is a cartoon, not a default.
3. **"Exponential forever"**: early growth is exponential only while S ≈ N; the logistic *is* the correction. Quoting r as if it persists overstates every projection.
4. **No tail**: the curve must decay to zero — immunity (recovery) removes infectives; drawing it plateauing above zero forgets recovery.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: one logistic, both curves</b></summary>

Commit to C(t) = K/(1 + e^(−r(t−t₀))) and differentiate once: the bell is C′(t) = Kr·e^(−r(t−t₀))/(1 + e^(−r(t−t₀)))² — its peak, its asymmetry corrections, and its inflection all fall out of two parameters. Sketching from the *equation* beats sketching from memory, and it scales to any single-wave outbreak.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: SIR without the closed form</b></summary>

The full SIR system dS/dt = −βSI/N, dI/dt = βSI/N − γI, dR/dt = γI has no elementary solution, but its orbits do: dI/dS = −1 + Nγ/(βS) integrates to I = N − S + (N/R₀)·ln(S/S₀) — the epidemic's entire trajectory in the (S, I) plane, peak and all, without solving a single differential equation. This phase-plane trick is the gateway to the qualitative theory of dynamical systems.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

Daily new cases: a single-peaked, typically right-skewed bell — exponential rise while susceptibles abound (dI/dt = I(βS/N − γ)), peak exactly when S = N/R₀, slow burnout to zero as susceptibles deplete; its integral is the cumulative logistic C(t) = K/(1 + e^(−r(t−t₀))) with inflection at K/2. The control knobs: R₀ sets peak height and the herd-immunity threshold 1 − 1/R₀ (flu ≈ 23%, R₀ = 3 ≈ 67%, measles ≈ 92%) — say which curve you sketched, and never let the exponential phase outlive the susceptibles.

</details>

---

#### Q27: Sketch rates of reactions (kinetics)

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — set the axes before the chemistry</b></summary>

Cover everything below. Announce the two graphs you are about to draw and their axes, out loud: **rate vs. concentration** (the *law* — how rate responds to [A]) and **concentration vs. time** (the *integrated* consequence — how the reaction consumes its reactant). Order 0, 1, 2 differ in both, and half-life is where the two views meet.

> Kinetics questions are testing whether you hold the differential law and its integral solution as one object. State both before sketching either.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "Rate vs. [A] — zero, first, second order. Three curves, one picture."</b></summary>

Sketch all three from the rate laws before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

- **Zero order**: rate = k — a **horizontal line**: the reaction is saturated (e.g. surface or enzyme-limited), extra reactant changes nothing.
- **First order**: rate = k[A] — a **straight line through the origin**, slope k.
- **Second order**: rate = k[A]² — a **parabola** hugging the axes, steepening fast.

The shapes get *more curved* as order rises; all three pass through (0, 0) — no reactant, no reaction.

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: [A] vs. time — integrate the laws</b></summary>

- **Zero order**: d[A]/dt = −k ⟹ [A] = [A]₀ − kt — **linear decline**, hitting zero at t = [A]₀/k (the line stops: the reactant is exhausted).
- **First order**: d[A]/dt = −k[A] ⟹ [A] = [A]₀ e^(−kt) — **exponential decay**, asymptotic to zero, never arriving.
- **Second order**: d[A]/dt = −k[A]² ⟹ 1/[A] = 1/[A]₀ + kt ⟹ [A] = [A]₀/(1 + k[A]₀t) — **hyperbolic decay**, slower than exponential at long times (algebraic 1/t tail) but faster early.

Three concavities: straight, concave-up-decay, concave-up-decay-but-fatter-tail.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — half-life, the order detector</b></summary>

Time to halve, from each integrated law:

| Order | t₁/₂ | Depends on [A]₀? |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | [A]₀/(2k) | yes — proportional |
| 1 | (ln 2)/k | **no — constant** (the hallmark of first order) |
| 2 | 1/(k[A]₀) | yes — inversely proportional |

The constant first-order half-life is why radioactive decay (first-order kinetics) has a *characteristic* timescale at all. Units of k differ too: concentration·time⁻¹, time⁻¹, concentration⁻¹·time⁻¹ for orders 0, 1, 2 — a dimensional check that spots a mislabelled order instantly.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **Constant half-life claim for the wrong order**: only first order has t₁/₂ independent of [A]₀; zero-order t₁/₂ shrinks with [A]₀, second-order grows. Cite the right formula for the order in hand.
2. **Axes confusion**: rate-vs-[A] for first order is a *line*; [A]-vs-time is an *exponential*. Swapping the two pictures is the classic error — the axes fix everything.
3. **Second-order tail**: 1/t algebraic decay — never quote exponential behaviour for a second-order reaction; its linearisation is 1/[A] vs. t, not ln[A] vs. t.
4. **Units of k**: forgetting that k's units change with order; a claimed "first-order rate constant" with units M⁻¹s⁻¹ is self-contradictory.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: the three linearisation plots</b></summary>

Each integrated law is linear in a special coordinate: [A] vs. t (0th), ln[A] vs. t (1st), 1/[A] vs. t (2nd). Experimental order-determination is exactly this: plot all three, the straight one names the order. One diagnostic idea replaces the memorised half-life table — and the same linearisation is how you *extract k* from data.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: Michaelis–Menten and saturation</b></summary>

Real reactions saturate: rate = V_max[S]/(K_m + [S]) rises linearly at low [S] (pseudo-first-order) and plateaus at V_max at high [S] (zero-order — the enzyme is working flat out). Michaelis–Menten kinetics is the interpolation between this question's first two rows, and the Lineweaver–Burk double-reciprocal plot is its linearisation — the same "find the straight line" philosophy as the ✨ block.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

Rate vs. [A]: horizontal (0th), straight through origin (1st), parabola (2nd). [A] vs. time: linear [A]₀−kt, exponential [A]₀e^(−kt), hyperbolic [A]₀/(1+k[A]₀t). Half-lives [A]₀/2k, (ln 2)/k (constant — the first-order hallmark and the reason radioactivity has a characteristic time), 1/(k[A]₀); k's units change with order (M·s⁻¹, s⁻¹, M⁻¹·s⁻¹). Experimentally: the linear plot among [A], ln[A], 1/[A] against t names the order and yields k.

</details>

---

#### Q28: Graph discussion — min/max, inflection points, possible equation

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — the eight-point audit, in order</b></summary>

Cover everything below. When shown an unknown graph, run the audit aloud and in order: (1) domain and range, (2) intercepts, (3) symmetry (even/odd/periodic), (4) asymptotes (vertical/horizontal/oblique), (5) monotonicity intervals, (6) extrema (local and global), (7) inflection points and concavity, (8) end-behaviour. The *order* matters: later items are cheap once earlier ones fix the scale and symmetries.

> The audit converts "what do you see?" into a protocol. Interviewers award the systematic run-through; a brilliant but unordered observation scores less than a complete ordered list.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "This curve has three turning points. What is the smallest polynomial that could produce it?"</b></summary>

Reason it yourself before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

A polynomial of degree n has at most n − 1 turning points (its derivative has degree n − 1, with at most n − 1 zeros) — so **degree ≥ 4**. A quartic with three stationary points can do it (e.g. x⁴ − 5x² + 4: derivative 4x³ − 10x, zeros at 0, ±√(5/2) — three turning points, degree 4). But beware the converse below: counting turning points bounds the degree *from below* only.

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: The reverse problem — features → equation, feature by feature</b></summary>

- Zeros at a, b, c ⟹ factors (x−a)(x−b)(x−c), i.e. y = k(x−a)(x−b)(x−c)(…): each real zero contributes a linear factor; multiplicity decides touch (even) vs cross (odd).
- Vertical asymptote x = a ⟹ a denominator factor (x−a).
- Horizontal asymptote y = c ⟹ degrees of top and bottom equal, c = ratio of leading coefficients.
- Oblique asymptote ⟹ degree exactly one higher on top.
- Oscillation ⟹ trigonometric core; exponential growth/decay ⟹ e^(±x) engine; alternating blow-ups ⟹ tan-type poles.

Assemble greedily: factors from zeros, denominator factors from poles, exponential/trig skeleton from behaviour — then let undetermined coefficients absorb the rest.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — and the honest caveat</b></summary>

The feature list rarely determines one equation: k is free, invisible factors (complex roots, squared factors) are free, and totally different species (rational vs transcendental) can share a feature list. The deliverable is a *candidate family* with reasons, plus the counterexample that keeps inference honest: f(x) = x⁴ + x² + 1 has degree 4 yet only **one** turning point — so "three turning points ⇒ degree 4" is a lower bound, never an estimate, and "degree n ⇒ n − 1 turning points" is false.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **Lower bound ≠ estimate**: degree ≥ turning points + 1; x⁴ + x² + 1 refutes any tighter claim. Say "at least".
2. **Zeros ≠ factors when cancelled**: a hole (removable singularity) looks like a zero but is a cancelled factor — check limits, not just the picture.
3. **Asymptote direction**: horizontal asymptotes are approached from a definite side; the sign of f(x) − c near the tails belongs in the audit.
4. **Inflection without extremum**: stationary inflections (triple-root style) have f′ = 0 but no extremum — do not count them as turning points when bounding the degree.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: Taylor-read the graph</b></summary>

Near any point x₀, the graph is its Taylor polynomial f(x₀) + f′(x₀)(x−x₀) + ½f″(x₀)(x−x₀)² + …: the intercept is f(0), the slope f′(0), the concavity f″(0) — the audit's items (2), (5)–(7) are just Taylor coefficients. A graph is a local power series wearing a costume; reading it that way turns "guess the equation" into "read the coefficients".

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: degrees of freedom and interpolation</b></summary>

A feature list of m independent conditions typically leaves a solution family with m fewer free parameters: n + 1 point-values pin down a degree-n polynomial exactly (Lagrange interpolation), while asymptote conditions and turning-point counts each consume specific freedoms. The theory of *inverse problems* — recovering an equation from observed behaviour — is the mathematical heart of system identification, and this interview question is its two-minute trailer.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

Run the eight-point audit — domain/range → intercepts → symmetry → asymptotes → monotonicity → extrema → inflections → end-behaviour — then assemble: zeros give factors, poles give denominators, asymptote degrees give leading terms, oscillation/exponential behaviour picks the species. Three turning points force degree ≥ 4 (quartic with three stationary points exists), but never claim more: x⁴ + x² + 1 has one turning point at degree 4, so turning points bound the degree from below only — and the honest deliverable is a candidate family with reasons, not a unique equation.

</details>

---

## 3. Algebra & Functions

---

#### Q29: Prove that n³ − n is always divisible by 6 (for integer n)

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — factor before you think</b></summary>

Cover everything below. First move: write n³ − n = n(n² − 1) = **n(n−1)(n+1)** — the product of three consecutive integers. Say what you see: divisibility questions about polynomials usually dissolve once the algebraic structure is exposed. The rest of the proof is bookkeeping about 2 and 3.

> The reflex "factor first" is the trained behaviour; the number theory is downstream of the algebra.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "Why must three consecutive integers contain a multiple of 2 and a multiple of 3?"</b></summary>

Argue both before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

- **A multiple of 2**: among n−1, n, n+1, the evens and odds alternate; with three consecutive terms at least one is even — indeed, either one or two of them are.
- **A multiple of 3**: residues mod 3 cycle 0, 1, 2, so any three consecutive residues are a complete set — exactly one of them is ≡ 0 (mod 3).

Both claims are pigeonhole in disguise: two pigeons (parity classes), three birds (consecutive integers); three residue classes, three consecutive integers.

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: Assemble the divisibility</b></summary>

n(n−1)(n+1) is divisible by 2 (an even factor) and by 3 (a factor ≡ 0 mod 3). Since gcd(2, 3) = 1, divisibility by both forces divisibility by 2·3 = 6:

n³ − n ≡ 0 (mod 6) for every integer n. ∎

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — and the negative-integer audit</b></summary>

The proof used only consecutiveness — parity and mod-3 residues — which are sign-blind. Formally: (−n)³ − (−n) = −(n³ − n), and 6 | m ⟺ 6 | −m. So the claim holds for **all** integers, negatives included; "for natural n" was the cautious hypothesis, and the proof earns the stronger statement for free.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **Negative integers forgotten**: the proof covers them, but only if you notice — say it aloud before the interviewer asks; the audit is part of the answer.
2. **"At least one even" understated?** No — but "exactly one multiple of 3" is the sharper, correct statement among three consecutive; use it: it shows you know *why* 3 divides the product.
3. **Coprimality skipped**: "divisible by 2 and by 3, hence by 6" requires gcd(2,3) = 1 (true here) — for divisors 4 and 6 the inference fails (12 divides neither 4·6-shared products automatically). Name the coprimality when you use it.
4. **Induction overkill**: induction works but conceals the structure; the factorisation proof is one line longer and explains *why* — prefer the explaining proof.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: induction as the fallback, not the engine</b></summary>

If factorisation had failed, induction would be the tool: base n = 0 (0 divisible by 6), step via (n+1)³ − (n+1) = n³ − n + 3n(n+1), where n(n+1) is always even, so the increment is 3·even = multiple of 6. Knowing *both* proofs — and choosing the structural one first — is what the interview is grading.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: congruences and Fermat's little theorem</b></summary>

The same argument in modular notation: n³ = n·n² ≡ n·(0 or 1) (mod 3) by Fermat's little theorem (n² ≡ 0 or 1 mod 3 — squares are never 2 mod 3), giving n³ ≡ n (mod 3), and n³ − n = (n−1)n(n+1) is visibly even. The general theorem nᵖ ≡ n (mod p) for prime p is this question's parent — and the companion fact n⁵ − n is divisible by 30 (5 comes from Fermat with p = 5) is the natural sequel.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

n³ − n = n(n−1)(n+1): three consecutive integers — one even (parity alternation), exactly one divisible by 3 (complete residue set mod 3); since gcd(2,3) = 1 the product is divisible by 6. The argument is sign-blind, so all integers are covered — and the structural proof beats induction here, with the induction step (n+1)³ − (n+1) = (n³ − n) + 3n(n+1) kept as the fallback that knows its place.

</details>

---

#### Q30: Prove that √3 is irrational

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — name the method and the lemma before starting</b></summary>

Cover everything below. State the architecture aloud: this is a **proof by contradiction** — assume √3 = p/q in lowest terms, and hunt for a common factor the "lowest terms" assumption forbids. And state the one load-bearing lemma in advance: *if a prime divides a square, it divides the root* (if 3 | p² then 3 | p).

> Announcing method and lemma first is exam hygiene: the interviewer then watches a proof, not a search.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "Assume √3 = p/q with p, q coprime. Square it — what does divisibility say about p?"</b></summary>

Drive the first implication yourself before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

3 = p²/q² ⟹ p² = 3q²: so 3 divides p². By the lemma (proof below), 3 divides p; write p = 3k.

Lemma, quickly: if 3 ∤ p then gcd(3, p) = 1; since 3 | p·p and 3 is prime, Euclid's lemma gives 3 | p — contradiction. So 3 | p. (This is the "prime divides square ⟹ prime divides root" step, and it is where primality of 3 is used.)

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: The descent and the contradiction</b></summary>

Substitute p = 3k into p² = 3q²:

9k² = 3q² ⟹ q² = 3k²

So 3 divides q², hence (same lemma) 3 divides q. But now 3 divides **both** p and q, contradicting coprimality. The assumption is false: √3 is irrational. ∎

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — the method's true scope</b></summary>

The argument needed: (i) a prime whose square forces divisibility by it, and (ii) the contradiction of common factors. Both survive replacing 3 by any non-square integer n — √6: p² = 6q² gives 3 | p² ⟹ 3 | p, p = 3k, then 3k² = 2q² forces 3 | q — contradiction. But it **fails for √4**: p² = 4q² gives p even, p = 2k, and then k² = q² — no contradiction, and indeed √4 = 2 is rational. The method proves: *√n is irrational whenever n is not a perfect square.*

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **Unproven lemma**: "3 | p² ⟹ 3 | p" is the hinge; cite Euclid's lemma (or prove it in one line). Asserting it without support is the most common gap.
2. **Contradiction mislocated**: the contradiction is that p and q share the factor 3 — against *lowest terms*. If the coprime assumption was never used, the proof has no target.
3. **"Even" reflex**: the √2-style "p even" argument does not transplant to √3 without naming the prime (3) and its lemma; composite √4 actively refutes the naive transplant.
4. **Converse overreach**: irrationality of √3 does not extend to "all roots are irrational" — √4, √9 exist; the correct scope is exactly the non-squares.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: unique factorisation in one line</b></summary>

In p² = 3q², compare exponents of 3 on both sides: the left has an **even** power of 3 (squares have even exponents in every prime), the right an **odd** one (3q² contributes one more than the even power inside q²). Even ≠ odd — contradiction, no p = 3k gymnastics. This exponent-parity view is the proof of the lemma and the main argument in a single glance.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: Euclid to Hilbert</b></summary>

The lemma "prime | product ⟹ prime | a factor" is Euclid's lemma, and the machinery underneath is unique factorisation (the fundamental theorem of arithmetic). Not every number system keeps unique factorisation — in ℤ[√−5], 6 = 2·3 = (1+√−5)(1−√−5) with all factors irreducible — and there the naive proof style genuinely fails. A century later, Hilbert's and Dedekind's ideal theory repaired exactly this. The two-line proof above quietly assumes a deep theorem.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

Assume √3 = p/q in lowest terms; p² = 3q² forces 3 | p (Euclid's lemma: prime divides square ⟹ divides root), so p = 3k, whence q² = 3k² forces 3 | q — both divisible by 3, contradicting coprimality. ∎ The same mechanism proves √n irrational for every non-square n (√6 works, √4 fails precisely because no contradiction arises), and the one-line exponent-parity view — p² has even, 3q² odd, power of 3 — is the same proof seen through unique factorisation.

</details>
---

#### Q31: Prove that when z² = x² + y² has integer solutions, x and y cannot both be odd

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — reach for the right modulus</b></summary>

Cover everything below. First, say aloud: parity questions about squares are best settled **modulo 4** (or 8), because squaring collapses residues — the proof will not track x and y individually, only their residues. Commit to mod 4 before computing anything.

> Choosing the modulus is half the proof: mod 2 only knows "even/odd" (too coarse — the sum of two odds *is* even, no contradiction yet), while mod 4 sees the square's *value*, not just its parity.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "What are the possible values of a square modulo 4?"</b></summary>

Compute them yourself before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

n ≡ 0, 1, 2, 3 (mod 4) ⟹ n² ≡ 0, 1, 4 ≡ 0, 9 ≡ 1 (mod 4).

**A square is always ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 4)** — never 2, never 3. Two residue classes survive squaring; that collapse is the entire engine of the proof.

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: Force the contradiction</b></summary>

Suppose x and y are both odd. Then x ≡ 1 or 3 (mod 4), and either way x² ≡ 1 (mod 4); same for y. Hence

z² = x² + y² ≡ 1 + 1 ≡ **2 (mod 4)**.

But Step 1 says no square is ever 2 mod 4. Contradiction — the assumption is untenable: x and y cannot both be odd. ∎

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — and the structure the proof reveals</b></summary>

The residues do more than refute: they classify. If x, y are not both odd, then (after swapping) one leg is even, and z² = odd² + even² is odd + even = odd ⟹ z odd. So every integer triple has the parity pattern **(odd, even, odd)** — exactly one even leg, odd hypotenuse. Checked against the family: (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (8,15,17), (7,24,25) — every one fits, and the proof *explains* why no counterexample can exist.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **Mod 2 only**: "odd² + odd² = even, but z² even — contradiction" fails: z could be even (e.g. 2² = ... wait, is there a triple with both legs odd? The proof says no — but the mod-2 argument alone doesn't see it: odd²+odd² ≡ 2 mod 4 is where the contradiction actually lives). Mod 2 is necessary but insufficient; name why you need mod 4.
2. **Residue table slip**: 3² = 9 ≡ 1, not 3, mod 4; the only survivors are 0 and 1 — check all four residues, not just the even ones.
3. **Conclusion overreach**: the proof forbids *both* odd; it does not say "one is odd, one even" without the follow-up observation that both-even is possible only in non-primitive triples (e.g. (6,8,10)). State the exact scope.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: mod 8 for free structure</b></summary>

Squares mod 8 are 0, 1, or 4. Odd² ≡ 1 (mod 8), so both-odd gives z² ≡ 2 (mod 8) — impossible — and additionally, with one leg even: even leg ≡ 0 or 4 (mod 8), odd leg ≡ 1, so z² ≡ 1 or 5 (mod 8) ⟹ z odd. One modulus up yields the full parity *classification*, not just the contradiction — and mod 8 is the natural home for the stronger statement that the even leg of a primitive triple is divisible by 4 (it is: x = 2mn in the parametrisation).

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: the complete parametrisation</b></summary>

Every primitive Pythagorean triple has the form (m² − n², 2mn, m² + n²) with m > n coprime, not both odd — from which the parity pattern, the divisibility of the even leg by 4, and even the " exactly one of every triple's three numbers is divisible by 3, and one by 5" facts all follow. The parameterisation is a rational parametrisation of the unit circle (stereographic projection from (−1, 0)) — the same trick that classifies all rational points on conics.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

Squares are ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 4) only; if x, y were both odd then z² = x² + y² ≡ 2 (mod 4), which no square satisfies — so x and y cannot both be odd. The same residue bookkeeping upgrades to a classification: every integer triple has parity (odd, even, odd), the even leg divisible by 4 in primitive triples, and mod 8 is the sharper modulus that gives both facts in one pass.

</details>

---

#### Q32: Prove that any integer is either prime or can be expressed as a product of primes

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — name the proof architecture</b></summary>

Cover everything below. State the plan aloud: this is the **existence half** of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, and the natural tool is **strong induction** — because a composite n splits into factors far smaller than n − 1, and only an hypothesis covering *all* smaller cases is strong enough to catch them.

> Naming "strong" before starting, and saying *why* ordinary induction is insufficient, is the mark being hunted. The proof itself is four lines.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "Why strong induction rather than ordinary?"</b></summary>

Answer it yourself before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

If n = ab is composite, the factors a, b can be *any* integers in (1, n) — say n = 101·103 = 10 403: the factors are nowhere near n − 1. Ordinary induction assumes the statement only for n − 1, which says nothing about a and b. Strong induction's hypothesis — "the statement holds for every k with 2 ≤ k ⋖ n" — covers a and b whatever they are. That coverage is exactly what the factorisation step needs.

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: The induction</b></summary>

**Claim**: every n ≥ 2 is prime or a product of primes.

- **Base**: n = 2 is prime. ✓
- **Strong hypothesis**: every k with 2 ≤ k ⋖ n is prime or a product of primes.
- **Step**: let n ≥ 3. If n is prime, done. Otherwise n = ab with 1 ⋖ a ≤ b ⋖ n; by the hypothesis, a = p₁⋯pᵣ and b = q₁⋯qₛ are prime products, so n = p₁⋯pᵣq₁⋯qₛ is a prime product. ∎

The well-ordering of the naturals underlies the whole manoeuvre: repeated splitting of composites must terminate at primes — there is no infinite descending chain of positive integers.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — existence is the easy half</b></summary>

The theorem students call "unique factorisation" has two halves: existence (proved above — everything breaks into primes) and **uniqueness** (the same n never admits two genuinely different factorisations). Uniqueness is the deep half, and it rests on Euclid's lemma: prime | product ⟹ prime | a factor — a one-line result with a two-thousand-year pedigree, and the load-bearing wall under both this theorem and the irrationality proofs.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **Existence vs. uniqueness**: proving "some factorisation exists" does not prove "only one exists" — conflating the two halves is the standard error; the lemma is what the second half needs.
2. **Weak hypothesis**: ordinary induction (assume n − 1) cannot justify the step for n = ab with a, b ≪ n; if your proof never uses the full strength, it isn't a proof — it's a lucky guess.
3. **Termination hand-wave**: "keep splitting" needs a reason to stop; the well-ordering principle (no infinite descending chain of positive integers) is the reason — say it, or the descent could be circular.
4. **Base case**: n = 2 is the true base (1 is the empty product — a convention, not a prime); starting at n = 4 begs the question.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: minimal counterexample</b></summary>

Suppose, for contradiction, some n ≥ 2 is neither prime nor a product of primes, and take the *smallest* such n. It cannot be prime, so n = ab with 1 < a, b < n; but a, b are smaller than the minimal counterexample, so each is prime or a product of primes — making n one too. Contradiction. This is strong induction in disguise (well-ordering as the engine), and it mirrors exactly how Euclid's lemma and the uniqueness half are proved.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: uniqueness, and where it breaks</b></summary>

Uniqueness: if p₁⋯pᵣ = q₁⋯qₛ, then p₁ divides the right side, hence (Euclid's lemma) divides some qⱼ, hence equals it; cancel and repeat. The lemma needs primality — which is why the proof fails in ℤ[√−5], where 6 = 2·3 = (1+√−5)(1−√−5) with all four factors irreducible yet non-associate: existence holds, uniqueness dies. Dedekind's ideals (1870s) restored uniqueness by factorising *ideals* instead of numbers — the birth certificate of modern algebraic number theory.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

Every n ≥ 2 is prime or a product of primes: strong induction (base 2; composite n = ab with a, b ⋖ n covered by the strong hypothesis over *all* smaller cases — which is why ordinary induction fails, the factors need not be near n − 1). Termination is guaranteed by well-ordering; this is only the existence half of the fundamental theorem — uniqueness needs Euclid's lemma, the same wall under the irrationality proofs, and the half that breaks in ℤ[√−5] where 6 factors two genuinely different ways.

</details>

---

#### Q33: What is the square root of x²?

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — two different √ symbols collide</b></summary>

Cover everything below. Before answering, separate the two ideas hiding in the question: (1) the **operation** of squaring — x² is never negative; (2) the **symbol** √ — which by definition returns the *principal* (non-negative) root. The question "what is √(x²)?" is where these two collide, and the collision manufactures the absolute value.

> The question looks insultingly easy — that is the trap. State the definition of √ ("the non-negative number whose square is…") before giving any answer; the definition is the answer.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "√9 = 3. So √(9) = √((−3)²) = … −3?"</b></summary>

Settle it yourself before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

√((−3)²) = √9 = **3**, not −3. The radical never returns a negative number — it returns whichever of {+3, −3} is non-negative. So the value of √(x²) depends on the sign of x:

- x ≥ 0: √(x²) = x (already non-negative — no adjustment needed);
- x ⋖ 0: √(x²) = −x (the flip makes it positive; e.g. x = −3 gives −x = 3).

Both cases say: √(x²) is the non-negative one of {x, −x} — that function has a name: |x|.

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: Verification and the graph</b></summary>

√(x²) = **|x|** — check: x = −3 ⟹ √9 = 3 = |−3| ✓; x = 5 ⟹ √25 = 5 = |5| ✓.

The graph is a V with vertex at the origin: slope −1 for x ⋖ 0, slope +1 for x > 0, undefined at 0. Note the moral: an expression involving a square root of a square was *not* smooth — the square root symbol smuggled in a corner.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — where the modulus really comes from</b></summary>

The piecewise answer is correct but unexplained. The absolute value appears because √ is *defined* to return the unique non-negative square root (see the ✨ block for the uniqueness proof). Two perfectly matched ideas — "squares are sign-blind" and "roots are sign-forced" — leave |x| as their only possible child. The same collision reappears wherever a square meets a root: √((x+1)²) = |x+1|, √(sin²x) = |sin x| — one principle, many costumes.

<details>
<summary><b>💬 Interviewer follow-up (round two)</b></summary>

**The interviewer:** "Fine for x². But what is √(x² + 2x + 1) — and what does its graph look like?"

Attempt it yourself — the trap has moved house.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

x² + 2x + 1 = (x+1)², so √(x² + 2x + 1) = **|x + 1|** — not x + 1. The graph is a V with vertex at (−1, 0): slope −1 left of −1, +1 right of it, corner at the vertex. This is the trap's true habitat: a *perfect square in disguise*, where the automatic "√(stuff²) = stuff" reflex writes y = x + 1, a straight line through the vertex — missing the V's corner entirely and flipping the left half of the graph below the axis. Bonus contrast: (√x)² = x is fine without a modulus — the domain x ≥ 0 already restricts the symbol to non-negative inputs; √(x²) has no such protection, since x² ≥ 0 for *every* x.

</details>


</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **√(x²) = x, obviously**: false for x ⋖ 0 (x = −3 gives 3, not −3). The formula is |x|, and the error is not algebraic sloppiness — it is forgetting the √ symbol's definition.
2. **Disguised perfect squares**: √(x²+2x+1) = x+1 is the advanced version of the trap; complete the square, then take the modulus, then sketch the V.
3. **(√x)² vs √(x²)**: the first needs x ≥ 0 and equals x there; the second exists for all x and equals |x|. Same symbols, different domains, different answers.
4. **Differentiability slip**: |x| has no derivative at 0 (corner); treating √(x²) as "just x" also erases this feature — the corner is the signature that the modulus is really there.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: uniqueness, not casework</b></summary>

The piecewise proof never explains *why* a modulus appears; this does. By definition, √(x²) is **the unique non-negative number whose square is x²**. Now: |x| ≥ 0 and |x|² = x². A non-negative number has at most one non-negative square root — so √(x²) and |x| must coincide. The modulus is the *uniqueness half of the definition*, not a bookkeeping artefact; and the same one-liner gives √(f(x)²) = |f(x)| for any f, with no case analysis ever.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: the modulus everywhere</b></summary>

|x| is the distance from x to 0, and |x − a| is distance to a: the modulus is the distance function of the real line, which is why it appears wherever a square root of a square does — in the derivative of ln|x| = 1/x, in ∫du/u = ln|u| + C, in the Fresnel-free integrals of |sin x|, in metric spaces generally. In complex analysis, |z| is the modulus of z = a + ib (length √(a²+b²)) — the same square-root-of-a-square in two dimensions, already forced to be non-negative by its very definition.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

√(x²) = |x| — the principal root is non-negative by definition, so x ⋖ 0 must flip to −x; verified at ±3, graphed as a V with a corner at 0 (no derivative there). The upgraded trap is √(x²+2x+1) = |x+1| — a V at (−1, 0), not the line x+1; and the deep reason, not the casework: √(x²) is the *unique* non-negative number squaring to x², and |x| is the only candidate — the same uniqueness forcing √((x+1)²) = |x+1| and √(sin²x) = |sin x| wherever a square meets a root.

</details>

---

#### Q34: How many ways of arranging the letters in BANBANBANANAS?

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — count before you compute</b></summary>

Cover everything below. First write the word and tally the letters with tallies, not memory: BANBANBANANAS has 13 letters with **A×5, N×4, B×3, S×1** (5 + 4 + 3 + 1 = 13 ✓). The tally *is* the data; most wrong answers on this question are wrong tallies, not wrong formulas.

> "Count first, then apply" — the tally discipline is the whole of Step 1, and it converts a recall question into a verifiable one.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "If all 13 letters were different you'd say 13!. Why is that too many — and by what factor?"</b></summary>

Find the overcount factor yourself before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

13! counts arrangements of *labelled* letters (A₁, A₂, …, A₅, …). Any real arrangement is counted once for every way of permuting the labels within each repeated family: 5! orders of the A's, 4! of the N's, 3! of the B's, 1! of the S — all producing the *same* visible word. So each real word is overcounted by exactly 5!·4!·3!·1! = 17 280, and

N = (13!)/(5!·4!·3!·1!) = (6 227 020 800)/(17 280) = **360 360**.

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: The division, done transparently</b></summary>

(13!)/(5!4!3!1!) = 6 227 020 800 / 17 280 = 360 360.

Sanity checks: the count is an integer (it must be — it counts something); it is smaller than 13! ≈ 6.2×10⁹ (repetition must reduce the count); and much larger than the 4! = 24 arrangements of the four distinct letters B, A, N, S (multiplicity expands it).

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — the general pattern</b></summary>

The multiset formula n!/(n₁!⋯nₖ!) counts arrangements of n objects with k families of identical items — "the factorial of the total, divided by the factorials of the repetitions". The division argument is the proof: label, count, divide by the labellings that look identical. This single idea covers anagrams, arrangements of "MISSISSIPPI", and the multinomial coefficient (n choose n₁,…,nₖ) itself.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **Tally errors**: the classic failure is miscounting frequencies (reading the word as 3 B's, 4 N's, **4** A's …). Write the tallies with running counts and check they sum to 13 before touching a factorial.
2. **Forgetting the 1!**: S appears once — dividing by 1! changes nothing, but writing the denominator *completely* is the habit that prevents real omissions when every family matters.
3. **Overcount reasoning inverted**: some divide instead of multiplying, or subtract the repeats (5+4+3) from 13 — neither reflects how labelling works; the correct adjustment is the *division by the internal orderings*.
4. **Non-integer results**: if your arithmetic gives a fraction, a tally or a factorial is wrong — the count of arrangements is always a whole number; use that as a free audit.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: build the word position by position</b></summary>

Divide and conquer without division: choose which 5 of the 13 positions hold the A's — C(13,5); which 4 of the remaining 8 hold the N's — C(8,4); which 3 of the remaining 4 hold the B's — C(4,3); the S takes the last slot. Product: C(13,5)·C(8,4)·C(4,3)·C(1,1) = 1287 × 70 × 4 × 1 = **360 360** — same number, no big factorials, and each factor is independently checkable. The identity C(13,5)C(8,4)C(4,3) = 13!/(5!4!3!1!) is the multinomial theorem in action.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: multinomial coefficients and entropy</b></summary>

The multinomial coefficient (n choose n₁,…,nₖ) is the coefficient of x₁ⁿ¹⋯xₖⁿᵏ in (x₁+⋯+xₖ)ⁿ — the expansion that generalises the binomial theorem — and it counts the ways n labelled balls fall into k labelled boxes with prescribed box counts. Its logarithm, divided by n, approximates the **Shannon entropy** −Σ pᵢ ln pᵢ of the frequency distribution (pᵢ = nᵢ/n): 360 360 ≈ e^{12.79} for 13 letters gives entropy ≈ 12.79/13 ≈ 0.98 nats/letter — anagram counts *are* entropy, made combinatorial.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

BANBANBANANAS: 13 letters, A×5, N×4, B×3, S×1. Distinct arrangements = 13!/(5!·4!·3!·1!) = 6 227 020 800 / 17 280 = **360 360** — 13! overcounts each word by the 5!·4!·3!·1! internal orderings of the identical letters. Equivalent constructive count: C(13,5)·C(8,4)·C(4,3)·C(1,1) = 1287·70·4·1 = 360 360. The tally comes first (it sums to 13), the result must be an integer, and the division-by-internal-orderings is the proof, not a recipe.

</details>

---

#### Q35: How many ways can 10 knights at a round table shake hands?

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — translate the constraints into structure</b></summary>

Cover everything below. First, restate the problem as pure mathematics: ten labelled points on a circle; join them in pairs by straight chords; **no two chords may cross**. The handshakes are a *non-crossing perfect matching* of 10 cyclically ordered points — and the crossing condition is what turns a routine count into the Catalan numbers.

> Naming the structure ("non-crossing perfect matching on a circle") is the unlock: the moment the problem wears its mathematical name, the known machinery applies.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "Consider knight 1. Who can knight 1 shake hands with — and why does that choice split the table into two independent problems?"</b></summary>

Find the recurrence yourself before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

Number the knights 1, …, 10 clockwise. Knight 1 shakes hands with knight 2k (must be **even**: the chord 1–2k splits the circle into an inside region of 2k−2 knights and an outside region of 10−2k; a handshake pairing an odd number of knights would strand someone unmatchable on one side — pairs require even headcounts).

- Inside: 2k−2 knights pair among themselves: C_{k−1} ways; outside: C_{5−k} ways.
- Choices multiply, and k runs 1 to 5:

C₅ = C₀C₄ + C₁C₃ + C₂C₂ + C₃C₁ + C₄C₀

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: Compute by the recurrence</b></summary>

Build from C₀ = 1 (no knights: one empty handshake):

C₁ = C₀C₀ = 1; C₂ = C₀C₁ + C₁C₀ = 2; C₃ = C₀C₂ + C₁C₁ + C₂C₀ = 5; C₄ = 5+2+2+5 = 14; C₅ = 14 + 5 + 4 + 5 + 14 = **42**.

Cross-check with the closed form: C₅ = (1)/(6)·C(10,5) = 252/6 = 42 ✓. The convention matters: seats fixed, knights distinguishable — 42. (If rotations were also quotiented out, a smaller count would follow; say which convention you use.)

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — the recurrence *is* the answer</b></summary>

Quoting Cₙ = (1/(n+1))C(2n,n) is acceptable; *deriving* the handshake recurrence is better, because it shows the Catalan structure comes from the single constraint "a chord splits the circle into independent regions". That same split-and-conquer births the closed form (generating-function solution of the recurrence) — and the square root √(1−4x) that appears there is a principal root, non-negative by the same definition that makes √(x²) = |x|.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **Off-by-one**: ten knights make **five** pairs, so the answer is C₅, not C₁₀. (C₁₀ = 16 796 would be the number for 20 knights.)
2. **Forgetting the crossing constraint**: with crossings *allowed*, the count is the number of perfect matchings of 10 points: 9!! = 945 — over twenty times larger. The constraint is the entire question; name it or the answer drifts.
3. **Odd handshake partner for knight 1**: pairing knight 1 with an odd-numbered knight strands an odd group somewhere; the parity argument is the recurrence's first domino — state it.
4. **Convention ambiguity**: 42 assumes fixed seats and distinguishable knights; say so, since "up to rotation" is a different (and harder) question.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: the recurrence derivation (kept from the source, tightened)</b></summary>

The alternative-approach block of the source is the strongest content available: derive Cₙ = Σ CᵢCₙ₋₁₋ᵢ from the knight-1 split, then *compute* C₅ term by term (14 + 5 + 4 + 5 + 14). Delivering the recurrence derivation when the interviewer asks "where do Catalan numbers come from?" outranks quoting the closed form — it converts a named constant into an understood structure.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: the Catalan universe</b></summary>

Cₙ counts an uncanny family of objects: non-crossing handshakes, valid parenthesis strings of n pairs (()() and (()) for n=2 — C₂ = 2 ✓), Dyck paths of semilength n, binary trees with n internal nodes, triangulations of an (n+2)-gon, and dozens more — all because they share this question's split-and-conquer recurrence. The generating function C(x) = (1−√(1−4x))/(2x) encodes them all; its square root is the principal branch, and its binomial expansion is how the closed form (1/(n+1))C(2n,n) emerges. One recurrence, a whole universe.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

42: number the knights; knight 1 must pair with an even-numbered knight 2k (a chord splits the circle into even headcounts), giving C₅ = C₀C₄ + C₁C₃ + C₂C₂ + C₃C₁ + C₄C₀ = 14+5+4+5+14 = 42 — matching C₅ = (1/6)·C(10,5) = 42. Traps: the index is C₅ not C₁₀ (five pairs); crossings allowed would give 9!! = 945 — the non-crossing condition is the whole question; and 42 assumes fixed seats, distinguishable knights, stated as the convention.

</details>

## 4. Discrete Maths

---

#### Q36: Painting cubes with five colours — how many distinct cubes?

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — identify the symmetry before counting</b></summary>

Cover everything below. First observation, stated aloud: naive counting undercounts, because two colourings that differ only by a **rotation of the cube** are the *same* cube. The problem is not "how many colourings" but "how many orbits of colourings under the rotation group" — and the tool is Burnside's lemma: count = (average number of colourings fixed by each rotation).

> Naming the symmetry group (24 rotations) and the lemma *before* counting is what separates this from a guess-multiplied-by-24 exercise.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "How many rotations does a cube have — and of what types?"</b></summary>

Enumerate them yourself before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

The 24 rotations, in five conjugacy classes:

| Type | Count | Fixed faces |
|---|---|---|
| Identity | 1 | all 6 (any face can go anywhere) |
| Face rotations ±90° | 6 | top, bottom (4-cycle the sides) |
| Face rotations 180° | 3 | 2 opposite faces; sides pair-swapped |
| Vertex rotations ±120° | 8 | none (two 3-cycles of faces) |
| Edge rotations 180° | 6 | none (three 2-cycles of faces) |

Check: 1 + 6 + 3 + 8 + 6 = 24 ✓. A colouring fixed by a rotation must be constant on each cycle of faces.

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: Burnside's lemma with five colours</b></summary>

A fixed colouring assigns one colour per cycle of faces; with n colours available, a rotation with c face-cycles fixes n^c colourings:

- Identity: n⁶
- ±90° face turns (c = 3): 6n³
- 180° face turns (c = 4): 3n⁴
- Vertex turns (c = 2): 8n²
- Edge turns (c = 3): 6n³

N(n) = (n⁶ + 3n⁴ + 12n³ + 8n²)/24. At n = 5: (15 625 + 1 875 + 1 500 + 200)/24 = 19 200/24 = **800** distinct cubes.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — and the exact-five follow-through</b></summary>

"All five colours used" needs inclusion–exclusion over missing colours. With N(k) as above: choose which 5−k colours appear, count N(k):

N_exact(5) = N(5) − C(5,1)N(4) + C(5,2)N(3) − C(5,3)N(2) + C(5,4)N(1)
= 800 − 5·240 + 10·57 − 10·10 + 5·1 = **75**.

So 800 distinct five-colourings (colours may repeat), of which exactly 75 use all five colours at least once.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **Plain division**: counting labelled colourings and dividing by 24 fails — rotations do not act freely (a symmetric colouring has a non-trivial stabiliser); Burnside exists precisely because fixed points differ by rotation type.
2. **Cycle-counting errors**: a ±90° face turn has **3** face-cycles (top, bottom, one 4-cycle of sides), not 4; the exponent in n^c is the number of cycles, not the number of fixed faces.
3. **Burnside vs. necklace confusion**: rotations only — reflections are *not* achievable by turning a cube in space (chirality matters), so the group has 24 elements, not 48.
4. **Inclusion–exclusion direction**: subtracting missing-colour cubes must alternate signs; forgetting the final +5·N(1) term (cubes using exactly one colour) undercounts the exact-five answer.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: brute-force audit for small n</b></summary>

With five colours and six faces there are 5⁶ = 15 625 labelled colourings — enumerable by computer in microseconds, and dividing *that* by 24 gives 651, not 800 — the gap *is* the stabiliser correction. Running the mental (or actual) Burnside average against a brute-force script is how you catch cycle-counting slips: the two methods must agree, and their disagreement localises the error.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: Pólya enumeration</b></summary>

Burnside's lemma upgrades to Pólya's enumeration theorem when the "colours" carry weights (e.g. count by the number of faces of each colour): the cycle index of the group — for the cube's face action, (x₁⁶ + 6x₁²x₄ + 3x₁²x₂² + 8x₃² + 6x₂³)/24 — becomes a generating function whose coefficients answer every such counting question at once. The same machinery counts chemical isomers (graph automorphisms), necklaces, and quantum states.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

800 distinct cubes with five colours available: Burnside over the 24-element rotation group, (n⁶ + 3n⁴ + 12n³ + 8n²)/24 at n = 5 — the cycle counts (6, 4, 3, 2, 3 across the five rotation types) doing all the work. Exactly 75 use all five colours: inclusion–exclusion 800 − 5·240 + 10·57 − 10·10 + 5·1. Plain division by 24 undercounts (symmetric colourings have stabilisers), reflections are excluded (rotations only, 24 not 48), and the exponent in each n^c is cycles, not fixed faces.

</details>

---

#### Q37: What is the maximum number of pieces a disc (pizza) can be cut into with n straight cuts?

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — find the increment before the formula</b></summary>

Cover everything below. First move: do not hunt for a closed form — hunt for the **increment**. Let f(n) be the maximum pieces; ask what the n-th cut can add. One new cut is a line segment (chord) across the pizza; each region it passes through is split in two, so the increment equals the number of regions the cut passes through.

> Recurrence before formula is the trained instinct for every "maximum regions" problem: lines, circles, planes, cakes — all answer to the same question "what can the newest cut add?"

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "So the n-th cut adds at most …? And when is the bound attained?"</b></summary>

Argue the increment yourself before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

A straight cut meeting the previous n − 1 lines inside the pizza is divided into **n segments** (n − 1 interior intersection points create n pieces of line), and it passes through n existing regions, splitting each — increment at most n. Attained when the n-th cut crosses all n − 1 previous cuts **inside** the pizza, with all intersection points distinct (no triple concurrence) — achievable by generic cuts (small tilts and shifts).

f(n) = f(n−1) + n, f(0) = 1 ⟹ f(n) = 1 + (1 + 2 + ⋯ + n) = 1 + n(n+1)/2.

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: Numbers and checks</b></summary>

f(0) = 1, f(1) = 2, f(2) = 4, f(3) = 7, f(4) = 11, f(5) = 16, f(6) = 22.

- Sanity: f(3) = 7 — not 8 (the third line cannot be cut into three *interior* segments by only two previous lines inside the disc).
- The increments 1, 2, 3, … are visible in any good sketch; the formula is just their sum.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — the pattern and its limits</b></summary>

Maximum pieces with n cuts: **1 + n(n+1)/2** — the "lazy caterer" sequence. Two honest caveats: "maximum" needs the generic-position condition (every pair crossing inside, no triple point); and the pizza's boundary matters only by bounding the cuts — the identical formula counts regions of the *plane* cut by n lines, since excess intersections simply fall outside the disc.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **Doubling reflex**: claiming f(n) = 2ⁿ (2, 4, 8, …) — the third cut fails to double because it can only add 3 regions, not 4; doubling dies at n = 3 where the geometric constraint bites.
2. **Increment without attainability**: "adds n" requires all n − 1 crossings to lie inside the pizza *and* be distinct; two parallel cuts add less, a triple concurrence adds less. Maximum is a condition, not a default.
3. **Off-by-one**: the cut is divided into n segments by n − 1 interior points — counting segments as n − 1 loses one piece per cut (the endpoints inside the boundary add the last segment).
4. **Formula mis-quoting**: 1 + n(n+1)/2, not n(n+1)/2 (forgets the original single piece) or (n²+n+2)/2 — same thing, but know the shape you mean.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: Euler's formula check</b></summary>

For n generic lines cutting a disc: the arrangement inside has V = C(n,2) interior intersections, E = n² edge-segments (each of n lines cut into n+1 pieces, minus the two exterior rays… the count is n·(n+1) − 2n = n² − n, plus boundary arcs n) — and Euler V − E + F = 2 forces F = 1 + n(n+1)/2. The recurrence is faster; Euler is the audit that catches recurrence slips. (For the plane, V = C(n,2) + n… the same machinery delivers the lazy caterer number as a special case.)

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: from pizza to cake</b></summary>

In the plane the identical formula counts regions of n lines (lazy caterer); in 3D the maximum pieces of a cake by n plane cuts are the "cake numbers" 1 + C(n,1) + C(n,2) + C(n,3) (1, 2, 4, 8, 15, 26, 42 — note 8 = 2³ then *under*-doubling begins). The general d-dimensional pattern, Σ C(n,k) for k ≤ d, is a theorem of convex geometry — and 42 appearing as the 5-cut cake number is a numerological coincidence best left unmentioned… or not.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

Maximum pieces with n straight cuts: f(n) = 1 + n(n+1)/2 — the n-th cut adds at most n regions (it is split into n segments by n − 1 interior crossings, each segment splitting one region), attained exactly when every pair of cuts crosses inside the pizza and no three concur. Sequence 1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, 22 — the doubling dies at the third cut (7, not 8); the formula is the lazy caterer number, identical to regions of n lines in the plane, with cake numbers Σ_{k≤3} C(n,k) as the 3D sequel.

</details>

---

#### Q38: An ant is at one vertex of a solid cube. What is the shortest path to the opposite vertex (on the cube's surface)?

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — the unfolding principle, stated as a theorem</b></summary>

Cover everything below. First, state the principle and *why* it is true: any surface path can be unfolded — the cube's faces rolled flat — into a path in the plane between the same endpoints; planar paths are shortest when straight (triangle inequality); so the shortest surface path unfolds to a **straight line** in *some* unfolding. The whole problem becomes: enumerate the unfoldings, measure the straight lines.

> The justification matters: it is not "unfolding feels shortest" but "unfolding preserves length and straightening minimises". Principle first, enumeration second.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "Unfold two adjacent faces. Where do the endpoints land, and how long is the straight line?"</b></summary>

Do the unfolding yourself before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

Let the cube have side 1, the ant at A and target at the opposite vertex G. Unfold the two faces sharing one edge of the journey: A and G land at opposite corners of a 1×2 rectangle — the straight line has length **√(1² + 2²) = √5 ≈ 2.236**.

This is a valid surface path (across two faces). Is it the best? Only if no other unfolding beats it — enumerate before concluding.

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: Enumerate the competing unfoldings</b></summary>

Three genuinely different configurations (any surface route crosses either 2, 3, or 4 faces; symmetric copies give equal lengths):

| Route type | Unfolded endpoints | Length |
|---|---|---|
| Two faces (across one shared edge) | (1, 2) rectangle corners | √5 ≈ 2.236 |
| Three faces, "adjacent" (two coplanar steps) | (2, 2) square corners… offset (1+1, 1+1) | √8 ≈ 2.828 |
| Three faces, "staircase" | (1, 3) rectangle corners | √10 ≈ 3.162 |

The minimum is **√5 ≈ 2.236** — the two-face route wins. Note the interior space diagonal √3 ≈ 1.732 is *shorter but forbidden*: the ant must walk on the surface. The temptation to quote √3 is the question's built-in trap.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis</b></summary>

Shortest surface path: **√5** times the side length — unfold the two relevant faces into a 1×2 rectangle and draw the diagonal. The method (enumerate unfoldings, minimise planar straight lines) is the general one: for a rectangular box a×b×c the candidates are √((a+b)² + c²), √((a+c)² + b²), √((b+c)² + a²), and the minimum of the three is the classic "spider and fly" answer.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **√3 reflex**: the space diagonal is shorter but violates the surface constraint — read the question's constraint ("on the cube's surface") and honour it.
2. **Single-unfolding conclusion**: computing only the two-face route and declaring victory misses the competition; enumerate all distinct unfoldings (2-, 3-, 4-face) before minimising — √5 wins, but the win is only meaningful against √8 and √10.
3. **Symmetry double-counting**: several unfoldings look different but are congruent by cube symmetry; collapsing to the three types above is the honest enumeration.
4. **Unfolding across the wrong edge**: the straight line in the net must connect the *unfolded* images of A and G — placing G's image carelessly (e.g. on the wrong face of the net) measures the wrong diagonal.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: box formula directly</b></summary>

For an a×b×c box, the shortest surface path between opposite corners is the minimum of √((a+b)²+c²), √((a+c)²+b²), √((b+c)²+a²) — the cube (a=b=c=1) gives √4·... all three coincide at √5? No: (1+1)²+1 = 5 in every arrangement — the cube's symmetry makes all three equal, so √5 is forced without case comparison. The box formula, learned once, answers cube, brick, and spider-and-fly alike.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: geodesics on polyhedra</b></summary>

Surface-shortest paths are **geodesics**: locally straight when unfolded (angle-in, angle-out with equal incidence across edges — Snell's law with equal media). On a cube the geodesic network between opposite vertices was this question; on general polyhedra, geodesics can pass through vertices (with total angle conditions), and the "shortest path on a terrain" problem is a staple of computational geometry (Mitchell–Mount–Papadimitriou's algorithm runs in O(n² log n)). Unfolding is the idea that launched the whole subject.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

√5 times the side length (≈ 2.236 for unit cube): unfold the two faces crossed into a 1×2 rectangle and take the diagonal. The method is enumeration-plus-minimisation — competitors √8 ≈ 2.828 (three faces adjacent) and √10 ≈ 3.162 (staircase) lose; the √3 ≈ 1.732 space diagonal is shorter but forbidden (surface constraint). For a general box the answer is min √((a+b)²+c²) etc., all coinciding at √5 for the cube.

</details>

---

#### Q39: Where does the force keeping something in circular motion point?

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — argue from inertia, not from vocabulary</b></summary>

Cover everything below. First, reason from Newton's first law: without force, motion is *straight* at constant speed. Anything deviating from a straight line is being accelerated, and acceleration needs force — so the circular motion itself *demands* a force. Direction next: where must it point to bend the path into a circle?

> The trained behaviour is inference from N1 (deviation ⟹ force) instead of recitation ("centripetal means centre-seeking"). Deriving the direction is the mark.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "Look at the velocity at two nearby times. Where does the *change* in velocity point?"</b></summary>

Do the vector geometry yourself before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

Velocity is tangent to the circle — its direction rotates with the motion. Take v₁ at time t and v₂ at t + Δt (same speed, direction rotated by Δθ). The change Δv = v₂ − v₁ points **toward the centre**: draw the two vectors tail-to-tail; the difference vector bisects them inward. As Δt → 0, Δθ → 0 and Δv points ever more precisely at the centre, with |Δv| ≈ v·Δθ and a = |Δv|/Δt ≈ v·ω = **v²/r** (since ω = v/r). Direction: inward, always.

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: Magnitude and provider</b></summary>

a = v²/r toward the centre: units check (m²/s²)/m = m/s² ✓. The *provider* is situation-specific — string tension (conical pendulum), friction (car cornering), gravity (orbits) — but the *requirement* is universal: bend the path at rate v²/r and you must supply v²/r of inward force. Break the string and the object flies off **tangent** (N1 resumes — it does not fly outward), which is the cleanest experimental proof that the force was inward and is now gone.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis</b></summary>

The force points to the centre ("centripetal" = centre-seeking), magnitude mv²/r. Two clarifications make the answer interview-proof: (1) *centrifugal* force is not a new force in an inertial frame — it is the *experience* of inertia in the rotating frame (a pseudo-force), felt but not exerted; (2) the force is not "caused by" circular motion — the causation runs the other way: the inward force *produces* the circular motion. Getting both directions of that arrow right is the whole answer.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **"Centrifugal throws it outward"**: in an inertial frame there is no outward force — after release the object goes *tangent*; the outward tug is a rotating-frame artefact, honestly labelled pseudo-force.
2. **Causation inversion**: "the object moves in a circle so a force appears" — backwards; the force (tension, friction, gravity) *makes* the circle. Force is the cause, curvature the effect.
3. **Direction drift**: the acceleration is inward even though the speed is constant — acceleration measures *velocity change*, and velocity is a vector; "constant speed ⟹ no acceleration" is the vector-blindness trap.
4. **Provider confusion**: mv²/r is the *requirement*, not the *source*; naming gravity when the provider is friction (or vice versa) loses the situational mark.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: the string-break experiment</b></summary>

One thought experiment settles direction, provider and causation together: twirl a mass on a string and cut it — the mass leaves *tangent*, not outward. Conclusions for free: the force was inward (its removal stops the bending), provided by the string (now absent), and the motion's curvature was the effect, not the cause. Experiments outrank wordplay.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: rotating frames done honestly</b></summary>

In a frame rotating with angular velocity ω, Newton's second law acquires two pseudo-terms: centrifugal mω²r (outward) and **Coriolis** −2m ω×v′ (deflecting moving objects — the trade winds, the Foucault pendulum, and the rotation of cyclones). Both are bookkeeping artefacts of a non-inertial frame, exactly as real as the frame is convenient; general relativity's equivalence principle later elevates the same idea to a cornerstone.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

Inward, always: deviation from straight-line motion requires force (N1), the velocity-change vector between neighbouring tangents points at the centre, giving a = v²/r toward it — supplied by tension, friction or gravity depending on the setup. On release the object flies *tangent* (cut-string experiment), proving the force was inward and now absent; "centrifugal" names an inertia-experience in rotating frames, not a new force, and the causation arrow points force → circle, never the reverse.

</details>

---

#### Q40: Coin flicking — one coin at another

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — state the idealisations before the conservation laws</b></summary>

Cover everything below. First, declare the model aloud: two identical coins, a frictionless table, a collision that conserves both **momentum** (always, no external impulse) and **kinetic energy** (elastic — the clean interview idealisation; real coins lose energy to sound and heat, and the conclusion changes). Assumptions on the table, then the physics.

> The laws are conditional on the model; saying so converts a memorised result into an argued one — and pre-empts the "real coins don't do that" objection.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "Write momentum conservation as a vector equation. What does elastic + equal masses do to the velocity *triangle*?"</b></summary>

Set up the vector triangle yourself before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

Momentum: **u = v₁ + v₂** (equal masses m cancel; u is the incoming velocity). Energy: u² = v₁² + v₂². The first says u, v₁, v₂ form a vector triangle; the second says the triangle satisfies Pythagoras with **u as hypotenuse** — and a triangle is right-angled exactly when its sides obey c² = a² + b² (converse of Pythagoras). So v₁ ⊥ v₂: the outgoing coins separate at **90°**.

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: The geometric picture</b></summary>

Momentum triangle: place v₁ and v₂ head-to-tail; their resultant is u. The angle at the join is 90°: a right triangle with hypotenuse u. In components (u along x-axis): v₁ = v₁(cos θ, sin θ), v₂ = v₂(cos φ, sin φ); conservation gives v₁cos θ + v₂cos φ = u and v₁sin θ + v₂sin φ = 0, and eliminating leads to (θ − φ) = ±90°. The picture is cleaner than the algebra — momentum energy together *force* the right angle.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — scope and limit</b></summary>

For elastic equal-mass collisions in 2D, outgoing velocities are perpendicular. Scope: idealised coins (elastic, equal masses, no spin, no table friction). Limits: real coins are inelastic — the angle collapses toward 0° (the struck coin absorbs the hit and the flick coin ploughs on); spin and edge effects break the idealisation further. The 90° result is the ideal's signature — beautiful, memorable, and conditional.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **One-dimensional reflex**: quoting "equal masses exchange velocities" — that is the *head-on* special case, where the outgoing angle is 0° and 180°... in 1D the "perpendicular" statement degenerates (one coin stops, the other takes u). The 90° result lives in 2D; know both regimes.
2. **Energy forgotten**: momentum alone leaves the angle free — the right angle is the *energy* condition's fingerprint. Dropping conservation of energy leaves the problem underdetermined.
3. **Real-coins overclaim**: genuine collisions are inelastic (and off-centre with spin); the 90° law is the elastic idealisation's prediction, honestly labelled.
4. **Momentum as scalar**: writing momentum conservation without vectors loses the geometry entirely — the result is a *vector* triangle fact.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: the triangle is the whole proof</b></summary>

Draw it: u as hypotenuse, v₁ and v₂ as the legs — momentum fixes the triangle's shape (head-to-tail sum), energy declares it right-angled (Pythagoras' converse). No components, no elimination, no algebra: the perpendicularity is visible in one diagram. When a result has a one-picture proof, give the picture.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: billiards, cradle, and scattering</b></summary>

In snooker, equal-mass ball collisions send the object ball along the line of centres while the cue ball deviates — the 90° law in action (ignoring spin, as the source notes). Newton's cradle is the 1D limit (velocity exchange). In particle physics the same conservation laws give the **invariant mass** of a decay: for a two-body decay, m² = (E₁+E₂)² − (p₁+p₂)², and the momentum-energy triangle reappears relativistically — the right-angle geometry is the classical shadow of a four-vector identity.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

For an elastic collision of two identical coins, the outgoing velocities are perpendicular: momentum makes u = v₁ + v₂ (vector triangle) and energy makes u² = v₁² + v₂² (Pythagoras' converse) — so the triangle is right-angled with u as hypotenuse, v₁ ⊥ v₂. Scope honestly stated: idealised elastic equal-mass 2D; the head-on limit is velocity exchange (1D), and real inelastic coins collapse the angle toward 0°. The one-diagram proof is the whole argument.

</details>
