### 7.2 Energy, Thermodynamics & Kinetics

---

#### Q60: Fridge in a thermally isolated room

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — the fridge is a pump, not a cold generator</b></summary>

Cover everything below. First, correct the mental model aloud: a refrigerator does not "make cold" — it is a **heat pump**, shovelling heat from its interior (cold reservoir) through the refrigerant circuit to the radiator fins at the back (hot reservoir). The shovel runs on electrical work W. The first law, not folklore, will decide the room's fate.

> Naming the device correctly (pump, two reservoirs, work input) is the conceptual mark; the arithmetic is one line.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "Energy bookkeeping: where does the electricity end up?"</b></summary>

Trace it yourself before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

First law for the room (isolated: nothing leaves): every joule of electrical work W is dissipated *inside the room* — Joule heating in the compressor motor and wiring, and the heat Q_C the pump extracted from the fridge interior, which the condenser dumps into the room air. Total dumped: Q_C + W. Nothing subtracts.

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: The verdict, with the why</b></summary>

Room temperature **rises** — steadily, by (Q_C + W) per unit time. The fridge interior cools, but the heat did not vanish (no heat leaves the isolated room); it moved, and the moving cost W. Net effect: the room gains exactly the electrical energy consumed. A fridge with its door open is a particularly honest electric heater with a cold corner.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — and the coefficient of performance</b></summary>

The same pump, honestly rated: a fridge's coefficient of performance COP = Q_C/W is typically 2–4 — it moves several joules of heat per joule of work. But *all* of Q_C + W still lands in the room; efficiency of moving heat is not exemption from conservation. The door-open fridge warms the room faster than a bare heater of equal *electrical* power would — it is heater-plus-pumped-heat — a fact that surprises exactly once.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **"Cold is removed"**: cold is not a substance — heat is what moves; the interior's cooling is heat *leaving*, which re-enters the room via the condenser. Substance-thinking ("the cold leaks out") is the root error.
2. **Forgetting W**: comparing only Q_C in and out yields "no change"; the work input is the entire reason the room warms.
3. **Isolation broken**: with a non-isolated room (a real kitchen), heat escapes through walls and the fridge merely delays equilibrium — the conclusion is conditional on isolation, and saying so is part of the answer.
4. **COP misread**: a high COP does not cool the room — it cools the fridge *more effectively per watt*, dumping even more total heat per second into the same room.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: track one joule</b></summary>

Follow a single joule of electricity: it becomes compressor heat, plus it buys the pumping of ~3 joules (COP ≈ 3) from interior to room. One joule in, four joules dumped — the room's ledger is (1 + COP)·W per second, all inside the boundary. Joule-tracking turns the first-law argument into arithmetic a child can audit, and it generalises instantly: any appliance in an isolated room is a heater (TV, fan, computer — all of them, always).

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: heat pumps as the grid's most efficient heater</b></summary>

Run the pump in reverse and call it a heat pump: delivering Q_C + W to a house per joule of electricity — an "efficiency" of 300–400% by the (misleading) marketing arithmetic, properly a COP. Heat pumps now heat buildings at a quarter the emissions of gas boilers, and their thermodynamics is exactly this question's: work in, heat moved, all joules accounted. The fridge and the future of home heating are one machine.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

The room warms: the fridge is a heat pump, not a cold generator — it moves Q_C from interior to back-fins at electrical cost W, and the isolated room receives Q_C + W with no exit. Joule-tracking: one joule in buys ~3 joules pumped (COP ≈ 3), dumping 4 joules total — a door-open fridge is an honest heater, and the same machine reversed is the heat pump that out-heats any resistive bar per joule of electricity.

</details>

#### Q61: Blowing on soup — physical mechanism and energy estimate

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — mechanism before numbers</b></summary>

Cover everything below. First, answer the qualitative question with the mechanism stated precisely: blowing strips away the **saturated vapour layer** hovering above the soup, replacing it with drier room air; the vapour-pressure gradient steepens, and evaporation — each gram costing the latent heat of vaporisation — accelerates. Cooling is evaporation-driven, not wind-chill on the liquid's bulk.

> "Wind-chill" is the vocabulary trap; the mechanism is mass transfer across a vapour boundary layer. Name it, then quantify.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "Latent heat of water? And how much cooling does one gram of evaporated water buy?"</b></summary>

Estimate both yourself before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

- Latent heat of vaporisation L ≈ 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg (at 100 °C; ~2.4 × 10⁶ J/kg at room temperature — quote either, own the choice).
- One gram evaporated removes ≈ 2 260 J from the soup.

Heat capacity of the soup: ≈ 0.2 kg × 4 200 J/kg/K ≈ 840 J/K. One gram of evaporation therefore drops the temperature by ΔT = 2260/840 ≈ **2.7 °C**.

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: The equilibrium that stops the cooling</b></summary>

Evaporation self-limits: as the soup cools, its saturated vapour pressure falls, the vapour layer thins, and the net evaporation rate decays exponentially toward zero — the soup asymptotically approaches the **wet-bulb temperature** of the surrounding air (the steady state where evaporative loss balances convective gain from the room). Blowing lowers the local humidity, pushing that set-point lower and accelerating the approach — which is why blown soup cools *toward a lower temperature, faster*, on both counts.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — and the sweat connection</b></summary>

Blowing cools soup (and skin) by the same physics that cools the human body: sweat evaporating at ~2.4 × 10⁶ J/kg carries heat away, and a breeze strips the humid boundary layer to keep it working. The fan doesn't cool the room — it cools *you*, by maintaining the gradient. One mechanism, three costumes (soup, sweat, cooling towers).

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **"Wind-chill on the liquid"**: the bulk liquid is barely affected by the breeze; the cooling is *evaporative* — the heat leaves with the vapour. Conflating forced convection over a solid with mass transfer over an evaporating surface misses the mechanism.
2. **Latent vs specific heat**: quoting cΔT for evaporation (≈ 4 200 J/kg) instead of L (≈ 2.3 × 10⁶ J/kg) understates the effect by a factor of 500.
3. **Cooling forever**: evaporation stops at the wet-bulb set-point; drawing the temperature curve as unbounded decline ignores the vapour-pressure feedback.
4. **Boiling confusion**: at 100 °C the mechanism saturates — below boiling, evaporation is a surface phenomenon driven by vapour pressure, not bulk bubbling.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: one number does the work</b></summary>

The ratio L/c ≈ 540 — evaporating one gram cools the whole soup by ΔT = L/(m_soup·c) ≈ 2.7 °C for a 200 g bowl. Memorise L/c ≈ 540 K·kg⁻¹ as "one gram evaporated ≈ half a kelvin per 100 g of liquid", and every evaporative-cooling estimate becomes one mental division.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: evaporative cooling engineering</b></summary>

The same physics sizes cooling towers (power plants evaporate ~1% of circulation water to dump waste heat), designs sweat-wicking fabrics by pore geometry, and explains the *swamp cooler*: air drawn through wet pads leaves cooled and humidified toward its wet-bulb temperature — refrigeration without a compressor, where the only fuel is the latent heat budget of water.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

Blowing strips the saturated vapour boundary layer, steepening the gradient and accelerating evaporation: each gram of water leaving the soup carries ~2 260 J of latent heat (L ≈ 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg — 500× larger than cΔT), dropping a 200 g bowl by ~2.7 °C per gram until the vapour-pressure feedback settles it at the wet-bulb temperature. Wind-chill-on-the-liquid is the trap; the fan cools the *gradient*, which is the same physics behind sweat, swamp coolers, and cooling towers.

</details>

#### Q62: Differential equations — "rate is proportional to amount remaining"

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — translate the sentence into mathematics before solving</b></summary>

Cover everything below. First move: convert the English into symbols aloud — "rate is proportional to amount remaining" reads dx/dt = −kx (the minus: *remaining* implies depletion). Stating the differential equation before any solving is the translation skill; the solution is then a known dance.

> Interviewers pose this sentence to test translation, not integration. Say the equation, identify k's meaning, and only then solve.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "Solve it — and what does the constant mean physically?"</b></summary>

Solve and interpret yourself before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

Separate: dx/x = −k dt ⟹ ln x = −kt + C ⟹ **x(t) = x₀ e^(−kt)**.

k is the fractional decay rate (1/time): its reciprocal 1/k is the *characteristic lifetime* (e-folding time — the time to fall to 1/e ≈ 37%); half-life t₁/₂ = ln 2/k. The answer is one exponential with two interchangeable time constants.

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: The graph and its half-life</b></summary>

x vs t: exponential decay from x₀, slope −kx₀ at t = 0, asymptotic to zero — never arriving. The half-life is *constant*: every t₁/₂ the amount halves (the "amount remaining" condition is scale-free — the same sentence describes the second half-life as the first). Checkpoint: x(t₁/₂) = x₀/2 ✓; x(2t₁/₂) = x₀/4 ✓ — geometric, not linear, decline.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — one equation, everywhere</b></summary>

dx/dt = −kx is the most reused differential equation in science: radioactive decay (k = ln 2/half-life), first-order chemical kinetics, capacitor discharge, Newton's cooling (near a fixed ambient), population decline, drug clearance in pharmacokinetics. The sentence "rate proportional to what remains" is its universal signature — recognising it on sight is worth more than re-solving it.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **Sign of k**: "remaining" demands the minus sign; dx/dt = +kx grows — the sign is part of the translation, and getting it wrong produces a population explosion instead of a decay.
2. **k vs t₁/₂ confusion**: k is a *rate* (s⁻¹); the half-life is ln 2/k — quoting k as a time (or t₁/₂ as a rate) is a units error invisible until someone checks.
3. **"Proportional" mis-set**: the sentence fixes proportionality *to the current amount*, not to time or to a constant flux; writing dx/dt = −k misreads the sentence as zero-order.
4. **Linearisation error**: sketching exponential decay as a straight line to zero misses both the asymptote and the constant half-life — the two diagnostic features.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: read k directly from the sentence</b></summary>

Train the reflex: "rate proportional to amount" ⟹ exponential, "proportionality constant" ⟹ k has units of 1/time, "half" ⟹ t₁/₂ = ln 2/k, "37%" ⟹ one e-folding time 1/k. No solving needed for any of these — the solution's *features* are readable from the sentence alone, and the explicit integral x = x₀e^(−kt) becomes confirmation rather than discovery.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: the linear system behind it all</b></summary>

The equation is the scalar case of the linear system dx/dt = Ax, whose solutions are sums of exponentials e^(λᵢt) — the reason eigenvalues govern vibrations, circuits, Markov chains and quantum decay. Laplace transforms turn such equations into algebra; the exponential ansatz x = e^(λt), which reduces the equation to λ = −k in one line, is the seed of the entire method.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

Translate, then solve: "rate proportional to amount remaining" is dx/dt = −kx, giving x(t) = x₀e^(−kt) — exponential decay with constant half-life t₁/₂ = ln 2/k and e-folding time 1/k. The features are readable from the sentence alone (sign, units, half-life), and the same equation describes radioactivity, first-order kinetics, capacitor discharge, cooling and drug clearance — one sentence, one exponential, everywhere.

</details>

#### Q63: Pendulum — small oscillations and the large-angle correction

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — set the model and its regime before any formula</b></summary>

Cover everything below. State the model aloud: a point mass m on a massless string of length l, swinging in a vertical plane with no friction or drag. Then state the regime: we will *linearise* the restoring torque — a small-angle approximation whose validity must be tracked, not assumed. Both statements are load-bearing; the interview is testing whether you know where the approximation lives.

> "Assume small angles" is not a formality — it is the approximation whose error budget the follow-up quantifies. Own it from line one.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "Torque equation about the pivot — then linearise."</b></summary>

Set it up yourself before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

Restoring torque: τ = −mgl sin θ. Equation of motion: ml²θ̈ = −mgl sin θ ⟹ **θ̈ = −(g/l) sin θ**.

The exact equation is *not* SHM (sin θ ≠ θ). For small θ, sin θ ≈ θ (the first term of the series), giving

θ̈ = −(g/l)θ — SHM with ω² = g/l.

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: Period, evaluated honestly</b></summary>

Small-angle period: **T₀ = 2π√(l/g)**. At l = 0.5 m: T₀ ≈ 1.42 s.

The approximation's error is systematic and *positive*: the true restoring torque mg sin θ ⋖ mgθ, so the true motion is slower — T > T₀ always. The next terms of the series supply the budget:

T/T₀ = 1 + (1)/(16)θ₀² + (11)/(3072)θ₀⁴ + ⋯ (θ₀ in radians, the amplitude).

Worked checks: at 20° (θ₀ ≈ 0.349 rad): correction ≈ +0.77%; at 60°: ≈ +7%. The clockmaker's rule follows: keep amplitudes under ~10° and the small-angle pendulum is accurate to a quarter of a percent.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis</b></summary>

The pendulum is SHM's flagship application: geometric nonlinearity (sin θ) tamed by a regime (small θ) in which the system is linear, isochronous (period independent of amplitude — to first order), and universal (mass cancels: ω² = g/l contains neither m nor the amplitude). The isochronism is Galileo's gift to horology — and the (1/16)θ₀² correction is the price tag, quoted above.

<details>
<summary><b>💬 Interviewer follow-up (round two)</b></summary>

**The interviewer:** "For what amplitude is the small-angle formula wrong by exactly 1%?"

Invert the correction yourself before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

Leading term: T/T₀ ≈ 1 + θ₀²/16 = 1.01 ⟹ θ₀² = 0.16 ⟹ θ₀ = 0.40 rad ≈ **23°**.

Sanity: at 20° the error was +0.77%, at 23° it crosses 1% ✓ — the scale is quadratic, so doubling the error takes only √2× the amplitude. Two remarks complete the picture: (1) including the quartic term shifts the crossing by less than 0.1° (the series converges fast); (2) above ~60° the series is the wrong tool entirely — the true period diverges logarithmically as θ₀ → π (the inverted pendulum takes forever to fall), a singularity no polynomial in θ₀ can capture.

</details>


</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **sin θ ≈ θ without a regime**: the approximation is valid for θ ≪ 1 radian, degrading quadratically; quoting T₀ = 2π√(l/g) at 60° without the +7% correction overstates the clock's honesty.
2. **Period inverted**: T ∝ √(l/g) — longer string, slower swing; and g enters inversely (a pendulum on the Moon runs √6 ≈ 2.45× slow — same length). Swapping either dependence breaks every sanity check.
3. **Mass included**: m cancels entirely — a hammer and a feather swing alike (Galileo's pendulum); any formula containing m has a mistake upstream.
4. **Amplitude in degrees fed to the series**: the correction θ₀²/16 uses **radians**; 20° = 0.349 rad, and feeding 20 into the formula overstates the error by (180/π)² ≈ 3300.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: the elliptic integral</b></summary>

The exact period is T = 4√(l/g)·K(sin(θ₀/2)), where K is the complete elliptic integral of the first kind — K(m) ≈ (π/2)(1 + m²/4 + 9m⁴/64 + ⋯), reproducing the series of Step 2 instantly and valid to θ₀ = π. One special function absorbs the whole correction hierarchy; the series, the 1% amplitude answer, and the divergence at θ₀ → π are all its Taylor portrait.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: pendula that changed the world</b></summary>

Foucault's 67 m pendulum (1851) demonstrated Earth's rotation — the plane of swing precesses at ω sin λ (15°/hour in Paris) — because the pendulum obeys an absolute reference frame better than anything else in the laboratory. Schuler tuning in inertial navigation sets pendulum period ≈ 84 minutes (the same magic number as the gravity train — a satellite grazing the Earth), and the seconds pendulum (l ≈ 1 m) literally defined the metre's predecessor. The small-angle pendulum is a two-line equation with four centuries of consequences.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

θ̈ = −(g/l) sin θ ≈ −(g/l)θ for θ ≪ 1, so T₀ = 2π√(l/g) ≈ 1.42 s at 0.5 m — mass-free, amplitude-independent to first order (isochronism). The approximation errs positive and quadratically: T/T₀ = 1 + θ₀²/16 + 11θ₀⁴/3072 + ⋯ gives +0.77% at 20° and ≈ +7% at 60°; the 1% crossing sits at θ₀ ≈ 0.40 rad ≈ 23° (quartic term shifts it ⋖ 0.1°), and the true period diverges as θ₀ → π. Radians in the series — always.

</details>

#### Q64: Young's double slits — fringe spacing and glass-plate shift

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — path-difference geometry before any formula</b></summary>

Cover everything below. First, derive the condition from scratch aloud: light from the two slits arrives at screen point P; the **path difference** δ determines the phase; constructive interference needs δ = mλ (fringes), destructive δ = (m + ½)λ (dark bands). Fringe geometry is entirely the geometry of this one path difference — no memorised Δy = λD/d until the geometry gives it.

> Derive-then-quote: the formula is the punchline of a two-line argument about a right triangle, and interviewers score the argument.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "Small-angle approximation on the geometry — what is Δy?"</b></summary>

Do the geometry yourself before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

Path difference at angle θ: δ = d sin θ ≈ dθ (small angles). Bright fringes: dθ_m = mλ ⟹ θ_m ≈ mλ/d. On the screen, y_m ≈ Dθ_m, so spacing

**Δy = y_{m+1} − y_m = λD/d**.

(632.8 nm, D = 2 m, d = 0.5 mm ⟹ Δy ≈ 2.5 mm.)

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: The glass plate — which way does the pattern move?</b></summary>

A plate of thickness t, refractive index n, over one slit adds optical path (n−1)t to that arm (the light slows in glass; the extra path is what matters). The zero-order condition — "paths equal" — now requires the *geometric* path from the plated slit to be shorter by (n−1)t: the whole fringe system shifts **toward the plated slit** by

Δ = (n−1)t·(D/d)

fringe-widths: with t = 2 μm, n = 1.5: (n−1)t = 1 μm ≈ 1.6 λ — the pattern slides 1.6 fringe spacings (about 4 mm on the screen) toward the plate. Fringe *spacing* is untouched — the shift translates the pattern rigidly.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis</b></summary>

Δy = λD/d for the spacing, (n−1)tD/d for the displacement — one geometry, two uses. Both rest on the same small-angle right triangle; the plate's effect is purely an extra optical path in one arm. This is also the operating principle of the **Michelson interferometer**, where a compensating plate exists precisely to make both arms see equal glass — the same shift, deliberately cancelled.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **Shift direction**: extra path in the plated arm forces the geometric path *shorter* on that side — toward the plate. The sign is geometry, not memory.
2. **Spacing vs shift conflation**: the plate translates the pattern; it does not compress or stretch it. Δy depends on λ, D, d only.
3. **n vs (n−1)**: the plate replaces air (n ≈ 1); the *excess* optical path is (n−1)t, not nt — using nt overstates by 2× at n = 1.5.
4. **Small-angle honesty**: sin θ ≈ θ needs y ≪ D; at Δy = 2.5 mm and D = 2 m the error is parts-per-million — but at large angles the exact tan θ must replace the approximation.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: the wavelength ruler</b></summary>

Reframe: one fringe width corresponds to one wavelength of path difference. The plate adds 1 μm ≈ 1.6 λ, so the pattern *must* move 1.6 fringes — counting fringes is measuring wavelength, which is how Michelson gauged the metre against light itself (the 1983 definition: the metre is the distance light travels in 1/299 792 458 s). Fringes are nature's interferometric ruler.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: interferometry's empire</b></summary>

The same two-slit idea, polished: gravitational-wave observatories (LIGO's 4 km arms sense ΔL ~ 10⁻¹⁸ m — a thousandth of a proton's width) are Michelson interferometers; the first exoplanet detections and modern optical lithography rely on phase-shift control at the sub-fringe level. Young's slits, scaled and servo-locked, are the most precise length-measuring devices humanity has built.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

Δy = λD/d ≈ 2.5 mm (632.8 nm, D = 2 m, d = 0.5 mm) from δ = d sin θ ≈ dθ with the mλ bright-fringe condition; the 2 μm plate over one slit adds (n−1)t = 1 μm ≈ 1.6 λ of optical path, rigidly translating the whole pattern *toward* the plated slit by 1.6 fringe widths (~4 mm) — spacing unchanged. Fringes are a wavelength ruler: count the shift and you have measured the plate's thickness to nanometre precision, the same principle behind Michelson's metre and LIGO's strain sensitivity.

</details>

#### Q65: Candle lit in a rotating spaceship

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — the equivalence principle stated, not waved at</b></summary>

Cover everything below. Begin with the physics principle, precisely: in a *uniformly* rotating frame, a stationary observer feels a centrifugal pseudo-force mω²r outward — identical in form to a gravitational force. The equivalence principle licenses treating the rotating ship as a habitat with "gravity" g_eff = ω²r pointing outward. Precision matters: this is true only for uniform rotation, and only an *effective* gravity — the equivalence is local and kinematic, not fundamental.

> "Gravity ≈ rotation" stated with its conditions (uniform ω, stationary observer) is the mark; the candle's fate follows from it in one step.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "So which way is 'down' for the flame?"</b></summary>

Answer before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

"Down" = outward, away from the rotation axis — the floor presses you outward (centripetal), the pseudo-force feels like gravity pulling you "down" toward the hull. A released object falls outward; a candle flame — hot, less dense than its surroundings — rises against the pseudo-gravity: **inward, toward the rotation axis**.

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: The flame's shape and the equivalence's limit</b></summary>

Shape: like an Earth flame upside-down — a teardrop pointing inward, fed by oxygen streaming outward (buoyancy inverted). The flame burns normally otherwise: chemistry is indifferent to why the gases stratify.

The limit of the equivalence: the pseudo-gravity is *radial*, not uniform — g_eff = ω²r varies with distance from the axis, so two candles at different radii feel different "gravity", and dropped objects do not fall along parallel lines (they trace curved paths in the rotating frame — Coriolis effects). A uniform gravity field is only mimicked in a small neighbourhood of one radius: the equivalence is local, exactly as the principle demands.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis</b></summary>

The candle burns inverted (flame inward), sleeps normally in every chemical respect, and thereby demonstrates the equivalence principle at zero cost: no spaceship required, only a rotating frame of thought. The flung-candle energy check below uses the same machinery with conservation laws alone.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **"Flames die in zero gravity" overreach**: flames do not need gravity — they need convection *or* diffusion; on the ship's rim there is effective gravity (buoyancy works), so the flame burns as on Earth, merely inverted.
2. **Equivalence overstated**: treating rotation as *identical* to gravity forgets the Coriolis terms and the r-dependence; the equivalence is kinematic and local — say so.
3. **Direction slip**: hot gas rises *against* the effective gravity — inward, toward the axis; a flame pointing outward has the buoyancy backwards.
4. **"Stationary observer" omitted**: the pseudo-force argument applies to observers riding the ship; an inertial observer describes the same physics as centripetal constraint — both views are correct, and naming your frame is part of the answer.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: the flung-candle energy check</b></summary>

The same conservation machinery answers the dynamics instantly: the candle's mass centre rides at radius l/2 from the corner (midpoint of the half-edge), moving at v = ωl/2. Its kinetic energy ½mv² = mω²l²/8 is already "spent" rotationally; if the candle detaches, its remaining chemical energy E burns as on Earth while the ship slows microscopically (angular momentum conservation pays for the throw). Energy and momentum bookkeeping, no integration — the candle is a small rocket whose launch energy is the habitat's spin.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: rotation as a laboratory for gravity</b></summary>

The equivalence principle's modern form (Einstein): a uniform acceleration is indistinguishable from a uniform gravitational field — the seed of general relativity. Rotating frames are its poor-man's version, and they genuinely display gravitational physics: the Coriolis term mimics frame-dragging (Lense–Thirring), and the r-dependent g_eff mimics tidal gradients. Ring-shaped space stations are designed by exactly this arithmetic.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

The candle burns inverted: uniform rotation creates an effective gravity g_eff = ω²r pointing outward (equivalence principle, local and kinematic), so buoyancy sends the flame inward, toward the axis — an upside-down Earth flame, chemically unbothered. The equivalence's limits are part of the answer: g_eff varies with r and Coriolis terms curve free paths, so only small neighbourhoods mimic uniform gravity. Energy check for the flung candle: E burns normally, the tangential throw (mω²l²/8) is paid by the ship's spin.

</details>

---

#### Q66: How long is a molecule of polyethylene? (alkane geometry)

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — find the invariant projection</b></summary>

Cover everything below. First, confront the mess: a carbon chain tumbles, bends and flexes; a naive end-to-end distance is meaningless. The invariant is the **maximum extended length**, and it decomposes into (number of bonds) × (projected length per bond). The geometry question reduces to one projection — and the tetrahedral angle supplies it.

> Decomposition before geometry: "the answer is a product; find the per-unit factor" — the recurring Fermi move, applied to a molecule.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "Tetrahedral angle ~109.5° — what is the projection of one C–C bond along the chain?"</b></summary>

Do the projection yourself before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

The extended zigzag lies in a plane with bond angle 109.5°; the advance per bond along the chain axis is the bond length times the cosine of the *half-supplement* of the bond angle: projection angle = ½(180° − 109.47°) = 35.26°, and cos(35.26°) = √(2/3) ≈ 0.816. With bond length l = 1.54 Å: **per-bond advance ≈ 1.26 Å**.

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: The polyethylene molecule</b></summary>

Polyethylene: 750 monomers ⟹ 750 carbons ⟹ **749 C–C bonds**. Maximum extended length:

L = 749 × 1.54 Å × 0.816 ≈ **940 Å ≈ 94 nm**.

Checks: this is the fully-extended limit — a real chain in solution coils (random-walk scaling: typical end-to-end ~ l√N, a factor ~27 shorter); but the question's maximum is exact.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — and the membrane segue</b></summary>

The chemistry check lands beautifully: an 18-carbon alkane (stearic acid, C₁₈, in soap) has 17 bonds: L = 17 × 1.26 Å ≈ 21 Å ≈ 2.1 nm — the known bilayer thickness of cell membranes (≈ 2.3–4 nm with head groups). One projection, one product, and a measured biological length agrees within the head-group convention.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **Bond count off by one**: N carbons carry N−1 bonds (749, not 750); the off-by-one is a 0.13% slip here but the *habit* of counting links vs nodes is the mark.
2. **Wrong angle**: using cos(109.5°) directly gives a negative advance; the projection uses the *half-supplement* 35.26° — the tetrahedral geometry must be drawn before the cosine is written.
3. **Maximum vs average conflated**: 94 nm is the fully-stretched limit; quoting it as the "typical" length overstates by an order of magnitude. State which you computed.
4. **Å ↔ nm slip**: 940 Å = 94 nm (10 Å = 1 nm); losing the factor 10 in the final conversion is the classic last-line error.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: the magic tetrahedral factor</b></summary>

The whole projection collapses into one constant: per-bond advance = l·√(2/3) ≈ 1.26 Å. Memorise "tetrahedral advance = √(2/3) per bond" and every zigzag-chain length (alkanes, polyethylene, polypeptide backbones) reduces to N·l·√(2/3) — one line, forever.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: random walks and rubber</b></summary>

Real chains coil: the end-to-end distance of an N-bond random walk is ~ l√N (the freely-jointed model), while the *contour* length is N·l·√(2/3) — polymers are springs whose stiffness and entropy are set by the ratio of these two lengths. Rubber elasticity is entropy stored in those coils: stretch the chain, reduce its accessible conformations, and it fights back — the thermodynamics of tyres is the physics of this question's two length scales.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

≈ 94 nm fully extended: 749 bonds (750 carbons, N−1 links) × 1.54 Å × cos(35.26°), where the projection angle is the half-supplement of the tetrahedral 109.5° and cos(35.26°) = √(2/3) ≈ 0.816. The per-bond advance 1.26 Å is the recurring invariant; the chemistry check is stearic acid's 17-bond chain at ≈ 2.1 nm matching membrane bilayers; and the honest caveat — a real polyethylene chain in solution coils to ~ l√N, some 25× shorter than the maximum computed.

</details>

---

#### Q67: Draw and name the structures of the isomers of C₄H₈O

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — count the degrees of unsaturation before drawing anything</b></summary>

Cover everything below. First move, stated aloud: DBE = (2C + 2 − H)/2 = (8 + 2 − 8)/2 = **1** — exactly one π-bond or ring. The hypothesis space is therefore two families: **carbonyls** (aldehydes and ketones) and **rings/enols** (cyclic alcohols, ethers, the enol tautomer). The count does not draw the structures — but it tells you when you have found them all, which is the actual interview skill.

> Enumeration without an inventory bound is wandering; DBE is the inventory bound. Count first, draw second, count again at the end.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "Family one: the carbonyls. How many?"</b></summary>

Enumerate them yourself before opening.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

Aldehydes: CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO — **butanal**; and (CH₃)₂CHCHO — **2-methylpropanal** (isobutyraldehyde). Two aldehydes.

Ketone: only one skeleton places C=O internally: CH₃COCH₂CH₃ — **butanone** (butan-2-one). One ketone.

Family total: 3 carbonyls.

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: Family two: the rings and enol</b></summary>

- **Ring alcohols**: cyclobutanol (4-ring); cyclopropylmethanol (3-ring with a CH₂OH arm); 1-methylcyclopropan-1-ol (OH and CH₃ on the same ring carbon); 2-methylcyclopropan-1-ol (on different ring carbons; cis and trans stereoisomers are distinct compounds).
- **Cyclic ether**: tetrahydrofuran (oxolane, 5-membered ring with one O).
- **Enol tautomers**: but-1-en-1-ol / but-2-en-2-ol — genuine constitutional isomers but, unlike the carbonyls, they tautomerise to butanal/butanone; list them with the caveat.

Full inventory: 3 carbonyls + cyclobutanol + cyclopropylmethanol + the methylcyclopropanols + tetrahydrofuran (+ enols, with the tautomerism caveat) — the count closes: every structure carries exactly DBE = 1.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — the discipline of the inventory</b></summary>

The mark is not the longest list but the *closed* list: DBE sets the budget (one π-bond or ring), the carbon skeletons of C₄ are few (straight, iso), and each placement of the oxygen (double-bond O, ring O, OH, ether O) is enumerated once. Finish by re-counting: every drawn structure has 4 carbons, 8 hydrogens, one unsaturation — the audit that catches both omissions and duplicates.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b></summary>

1. **Stopping at the carbonyls**: 3 carbonyls is the comfortable answer; the rings (cyclobutanol, cyclopropylmethanol, THF) require the DBE budget spent as a ring rather than a π-bond — the family most often missed.
2. **Double-counting tautomers**: the enols are constitutionally valid but not isolable (tautomerism to the carbonyl); list them as a caveat, not as equals of butanal.
3. **Stereoisomers vs constitutional**: cis/trans-2-methylcyclopropanol are two compounds; counting them as one undercounts, treating them as different skeletons overcomplicates — know which game you are playing (constitutional enumeration first).
4. **DBE arithmetic**: (2×4 + 2 − 8)/2 = 1, using the oxygen-free formula (O atoms are invisible to the count); including oxygen in the numerator corrupts every count downstream.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: the bond-line audit</b></summary>

Draw everything skeletal in one row: butanal, 2-methylpropanal, butanone | cyclobutanol, cyclopropyl-CH₂OH, the methylcyclopropanols, THF | (enols). Then audit each in five seconds: carbons = 4 (count vertices), hydrogens = 8 (valence check), DBE = 1 (one ring or one double bond). A two-minute skeletal audit beats a ten-minute name-list every time — and it is exactly how a chemist checks an exam answer.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: why isomers matter</b></summary>

Constitutional isomerism is the reason chemistry is not algebra: C₄H₈O's families span flavourings (butanal), solvents (THF, butanone) and metabolic intermediates (enols as enzyme-transition-state analogues). The DBE inventory generalises to mass-spectrometry problem-solving — an unknown's molecular formula plus its unsaturation budget prunes the candidate structures before any spectrum is read. One count, three sciences.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b></summary>

C₄H₈O carries DBE = 1: carbonyl family — butanal, 2-methylpropanal, butanone (3); ring family — cyclobutanol, cyclopropylmethanol, the methylcyclopropanols (cis/trans), tetrahydrofuran; plus the enol tautomers with the honest caveat that they revert to the carbonyls. The method is the message: DBE sets the inventory budget, the skeletons of C₄ are few, and the closing audit — 4 carbons, 8 hydrogens, one unsaturation on every structure — is what makes the list complete rather than merely long.

</details>

## Extended: Oxbridge Interview Problems (Official Guidance & Recollections)

#### Q68: The Area of Region R (T1-15)

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — intersections first, geometry before calculus</b>
</summary>

Cover everything below. Say the plan aloud: a region between two curves starts at the intersection points; then integrate (upper − lower); and because one curve is a circle, hold a geometric decomposition in reserve as the audit layer.

> The candidate recollection behind this question reports the real interview walking through exactly this structure — the examiner wants the *plan* spoken before the integral is computed.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "G1. A region R of the (x, y) plane is defined as follows. It has x > 0 and y > 0. Its boundary consists of finite sections of the following three curves: the y axis, the curve y = x\^2 and a circle of radius sqrt(2) centred on the origin. What is the area of R?"</b>
</summary>

Attempt it yourself before opening anything.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

- Intersections: set x² = √(2 − x²). Solve for x² — what positive solution do you get?
- On [0, 1], which curve lies above? Check the easy point x = 0.
- The circular part of the integral is a standard form — or decompose it as a sector plus a triangle.

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: Find, order, integrate, audit</b>
</summary>

*Step 1 — intersections.* x² = √(2 − x²) → x⁴ + x² − 2 = 0 → (x² − 1)(x² + 2) = 0 → x² = 1 → x = ±1; in the first quadrant the intersection is (1, 1).

*Step 2 — which curve is upper on [0, 1]?* At x = 0: circle gives √2 ≈ 1.41, parabola gives 0 — the circle lies above throughout [0, 1] (they meet only at x = 1).

*Step 3 — integrate.* A = ∫₀¹ [√(2 − x²) − x²] dx. The standard integral: ∫√(2 − x²) dx = (x/2)√(2 − x²) + arcsin(x/√2), which at x = 1 gives 1/2 + π/4 (at x = 0, zero). And ∫₀¹ x² dx = 1/3. So

A = (1/2 + π/4) − 1/3 = **π/4 + 1/6 ≈ 0.952**.

*Step 4 — geometric audit.* The circular segment above the parabola splits as: the 45° sector of the circle (area π·(√2)²·(45/360) = π/4) plus the right triangle below the chord from (0,0) to (1,1) (area 1/2), minus the area under the parabola (1/3): π/4 + 1/2 − 1/3 = π/4 + 1/6. Same number, different route.

Self-check: 0.952 sits sensibly between the quarter-disc area (π/2 ≈ 1.57) and the triangle (1/2); both routes agree to the last digit ✓.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — plan, compute, audit</b>
</summary>

The mark is the three-layer discipline: intersections before integrals, (upper − lower) with the order justified at an easy point, and a geometric decomposition as an independent audit. When one boundary is a circle, geometry is not a luxury — it is the fastest check available, and saying so aloud is interview gold.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b>
</summary>

1. **Careless squaring** — x⁴ + x² − 2 = 0 in u = x² gives u = 1 or u = −2; the negative root is impossible for a square, and the region in question lives in the first quadrant.
2. **Integrating bottom-minus-top** — a negative "area" is a sign that the order was never justified; check x = 0.
3. **No geometric audit** — the sector-plus-triangle decomposition is the examiner's own route; omitting it leaves the calculus unverified.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: geometry first</b>
</summary>

The circular part of the area is *exactly* a 45° sector plus a triangle — π/4 + 1/2 — and only the parabola piece needs calculus: minus 1/3. A = π/4 + 1/6 by geometry with a one-line integral, and the integral route then serves as its own check. When a graph is drawn, the geometric plan deserves to be spoken first.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: one formula behind both routes</b>
</summary>

A = ∫(top − bottom) dx is the master formula; the trigonometric substitution x = √2 sin θ turns the circular part into ∫2 cos²θ dθ, and the geometric decomposition is the same identity read as areas. The meta-lesson from the recollection: when the interviewer supplies a graph, narrate the geometric reading before touching the integral — it demonstrates command of both routes.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b>
</summary>

A = ∫₀¹ [√(2 − x²) − x²] dx = (1/2 + π/4) − 1/3 = **π/4 + 1/6 ≈ 0.952**. Intersections at (±1, 1); the circle lies above the parabola on [0, 1] (checked at x = 0). Geometric audit: 45° sector (π/4) + right triangle (1/2) − under-parabola (1/3). Two independent routes, one number.

</details>

---

#### Q69: The arctan(x) + arctan(1/x) Trap (T1-16)

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — test the identity before trusting it</b>
</summary>

Cover everything below. Say first: the tempting move is the arctan addition formula — so test it before using it. Plug in x = 1 and x = −1: if a single formula gave one constant, both would have to agree, and they do not.

> A sketch question with no calculus is usually a hypothesis-testing question in disguise: the graph exists to punish blind formula use.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "G2. Sketch the graph of f(x) = arctan(x) + arctan(1/x)."</b>
</summary>

Attempt it yourself before opening anything.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

- Candidate identity: arctan a + arctan b = arctan((a + b)/(1 − ab)). What happens to its denominator when b = 1/a?
- Compute f(1) and f(−1) directly. What two values do you get?
- For x > 0, write arctan(1/x) in terms of arctan x — which complementary-angle identity applies?

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: Break the formula, patch by quadrant, verify</b>
</summary>

*Step 1 — the formula fails.* With a = x, b = 1/x: the denominator 1 − ab = 1 − x·(1/x) = 0 identically. The addition formula is a conditional statement, and its hypothesis never holds here.

*Step 2 — patch by quadrant.* For x > 0: let u = arctan x ∈ (0, π/2); then 1/x is the reciprocal, and arctan(1/x) = π/2 − u (complementary angles: arctan t + arctan(1/t) = π/2 for t > 0). So f(x) = π/2, constant on x > 0. For x ⋖ 0: both terms are odd, so f(x) = −π/2, constant on x ⋖ 0.

*Step 3 — assemble the graph.* Two horizontal half-lines: y = π/2 for x > 0 and y = −π/2 for x ⋖ 0, with x = 0 excluded (1/x undefined). As x → 0⁺, f → π/2; as x → 0⁻, f → −π/2: a jump discontinuity of magnitude π at the y-axis.

*Step 4 — verify.* f(1) = π/4 + π/4 = π/2 ✓; f(−1) = −π/2 ✓; derivative where defined: 1/(1 + x²) + (−1/x²)/(1 + 1/x²) = 1/(1 + x²) − 1/(1 + x²) = 0 ✓ — each piece is genuinely constant.

Self-check: the two direct evaluations kill any single-constant story; the zero derivative confirms the constant pieces; the gap at 0 is mandatory, not decorative ✓.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — conditionals have conditions</b>
</summary>

The entire question is one lesson: a standard identity is a conditional theorem, and the condition (here, ab ≠ 1) can fail identically. Testing the hypothesis at x = ±1 before using the formula is the mathematical habit being examined — the sketch itself is two straight lines and a jump.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b>
</summary>

1. **Asserting the addition formula unconditionally** — the denominator 1 − ab vanishes identically when b = 1/a; that degeneracy is the point of the question.
2. **One straight line through x = 0** — f(0) is undefined (1/x), and the jump of π between the two half-lines is the feature the sketch must show.
3. **Ignoring odd symmetry** — f is odd (both terms are), so the negative half-line is forced to −π/2; failing to use this doubles the work and risks inconsistency.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: two values first</b>
</summary>

f(1) = π/2 and f(−1) = −π/2, computed in seconds, instantly destroy the single-constant story; the complementary-angle identity then gives the two half-lines, and the graph is finished before the addition formula has finished failing. Test values before formulas — that order is the mark.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: the branch correction</b>
</summary>

The full statement: arctan a + arctan b = arctan((a + b)/(1 − ab)) + π·k, where k counts branch crossings of the argument; for ab > 1 the correction is ±π depending on the sign of a. The deep reason is the branch cut of the complex logarithm — ln z = ln|z| + i·arg z — of which the arctan addition law is the real shadow. None of this is needed; naming the conditional nature of the formula is enough.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b>
</summary>

f(x) = π/2 for x > 0, −π/2 for x ⋖ 0, undefined at 0: two horizontal half-lines with a jump discontinuity of π at the y-axis. The naive addition formula fails because its denominator 1 − x·(1/x) vanishes identically; the patch is branch-aware: for x > 0, arctan(1/x) = π/2 − arctan x; for x ⋖ 0, = −π/2 − arctan x. Checks: f(±1) = ±π/2; derivative ≡ 0 on each piece. One lesson: identities are conditional statements — test the hypothesis first.

</details>

---

#### Q70: A Medical Screening Test (T1-17)

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — pin down the question before computing</b>
</summary>

Cover everything below. Say first: "95% accurate" is ambiguous, so pin it down — take it to mean sensitivity = specificity = 95% (the test is right 95% of the time whether or not you have the condition). Then, before any formula, build the frequency table for a fixed population; the arithmetic is trivial and the interpretation is the exam.

> The verb is "discuss" — the number is the entry ticket, not the answer. The examiner wants to hear why a 95%-accurate test gives a surprisingly small probability.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "G3. A certain medical condition affects one in a thousand of the population. A screening procedure is developed that is 95% accurate. Discuss the probability that you have the condition if the screening procedure says that you do."</b>
</summary>

Attempt it yourself before opening anything.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

- Build a 2 × 2 table for 100,000 people: how many have the condition? Of those, how many test positive? Of those without, how many test positive?
- The question asks P(condition | positive) — which cells of the table answer it?
- What happens to the false positives if a second, independent test also comes back positive?

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: Frequency table, Bayes, retest, discuss</b>
</summary>

*Step 1 — the table (100,000 people).* Condition prevalence 1 in 1,000 → 100 affected, 99,900 unaffected. Sensitivity 95% → true positives 95, false negatives 5. Specificity 95% → false positives 5% × 99,900 = 4,995; true negatives 94,905.

*Step 2 — the requested probability.* P(condition | positive) = 95 / (95 + 4,995) = 95 / 5,090 ≈ **1.9%**.

*Step 3 — Bayes in symbols.* (0.95 × 0.001) / (0.95 × 0.001 + 0.05 × 0.999) = 0.00095 / 0.0509 ≈ 0.019 — the table *is* Bayes' theorem written out.

*Step 4 — a second positive test.* Independence: numerator 0.95² × 0.001 = 0.0009025; denominator adds 0.05² × 0.999 = 0.0024975 → 0.0009025 / 0.0034 ≈ **27%** — ten times higher, still far from certainty.

*Step 5 — the discuss layer.* "95% accurate" describes P(+ | condition), not P(condition | +) — the two conditional probabilities answer different questions, and confusing them is the base-rate fallacy. Because the condition is rare, the false positives (4,995) swamp the true positives (95): any positive is far more likely to be a false alarm than the real thing. This is why screening targets high-risk groups and why positives are always confirmed by retesting.

Self-check: 1.9% ≪ 95% is the entire point of the question; the two routes (table, formula) agree exactly ✓.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — the fallacy is the answer</b>
</summary>

The computation is four multiplications; the question is a test of interpretation. The base-rate fallacy — equating P(+ | condition) with P(condition | +) — is one of the most consequential reasoning errors in medicine and public communication, and this interview question is its purest form. The 2 × 2 table is the antidote that fits in six lines.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b>
</summary>

1. **Equating "95% accurate" with the answer** — the trap itself: P(+ | condition) = 95% says nothing directly about P(condition | +).
2. **Ignoring the base rate** — with a 1-in-1,000 condition, false positives outnumber true positives fifty-to-one; dropping the prevalence turns 1.9% into 95%.
3. **Stopping at the number** — "discuss" demands the why: the two conditional probabilities, the false-positive flood, the retest protocol.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: the 2 × 2 table first</b>
</summary>

For 100,000 people: 95 true positives against 4,995 false positives — so 95/5,090 ≈ 1.9% without writing Bayes' theorem at all. The table makes the false-positive flood visible; Bayes is then just the table in symbols. Concrete population first, formula second: that order is the mark.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: odds form and likelihood ratios</b>
</summary>

Bayes in odds form: posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio. Here: prior odds 1 : 999, likelihood ratio 0.95/0.05 = 19 → posterior odds 19 : 999 ≈ 1 : 52.6, i.e. ≈ 1.9%. The retest logic is the same multiply-again: a second independent positive squares the likelihood ratio. This is the machinery behind every clinical screening protocol.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b>
</summary>

With sensitivity = specificity = 95% and prevalence 1/1000: among 100,000 people, 95 true positives versus 4,995 false positives → P(condition | positive) = 95/5,090 ≈ **1.9%** (Bayes: 0.00095/0.0509). A second independent positive raises this to ≈ 27%. The discussion: 95% accuracy describes P(+ | condition), not P(condition | +); rare conditions produce positive tests dominated by false alarms — hence targeted screening and mandatory confirmatory retesting.

</details>

---

#### Q71: The Painted Middle Rung of a Falling Ladder (T2-06)

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — name the coordinates, find the constraint</b>
</summary>

Cover everything below. Say first: a locus question starts with coordinates — call the foot (s, 0) and the top (0, t); the ladder's fixed length gives the constraint s² + t² = L², and the rung's position is then pure algebra.

> The examiner's hidden agenda is classical: this is the trammel of Archimedes in disguise, and the midpoint special case has a one-theorem proof.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "Imagine a ladder leaning against a vertical wall with its feet on the ground. The middle rung of the ladder has been painted a different colour on the side, so that we can see it when we look at the ladder from the side on. What shape does that middle rung trace out as the ladder falls to the floor?"</b>
</summary>

Attempt it yourself before opening anything.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

- The ladder is a right triangle with the wall and the ground: what does Pythagoras say about s and t?
- The middle rung is the midpoint of the hypotenuse — where is it in terms of s and t?
- Substitute and recognise the conic. What is the radius, and what arc does the physical fall actually cover?

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: Constraint → midpoint → conic → arc</b>
</summary>

*Step 1 — constraint.* Foot (s, 0), top (0, t): the ladder's length L is fixed, so s² + t² = L² throughout the fall.

*Step 2 — the rung.* The middle rung is the midpoint of the ladder: M = (X, Y) = (s/2, t/2), so s = 2X, t = 2Y.

*Step 3 — substitute.* (2X)² + (2Y)² = L² → X² + Y² = (L/2)²: a **circle of radius L/2 centred at the wall-floor corner**.

*Step 4 — the physical arc.* The ladder starts vertical (s = 0, t = L: rung at (0, L/2)) and ends flat (s = L, t = 0: rung at (L/2, 0)); the fall sweeps only the quarter arc in the first quadrant.

*Step 5 — one-theorem audit.* In a right triangle the midpoint of the hypotenuse is equidistant from all three vertices — so the rung stays exactly L/2 from the corner for every position, instantly. At 45°: M = (L/(2√2), L/(2√2)), and X² + Y² = L²/8 + L²/8 = L²/4 ✓.

Self-check: endpoints sit on the locus; the midpoint-of-hypotenuse theorem reproduces the same radius; no force law was needed — the path is kinematic, not dynamic ✓.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — locus from constraint</b>
</summary>

The method generalises: name coordinates, state the constraint, eliminate. What looks like a mechanics problem is analytic geometry — the falling motion only selects which arc of the circle is traced. The classical name (trammel of Archimedes) and the one-theorem proof are the discussion-layer marks.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b>
</summary>

1. **Guessing "parabola"** — the visual association of falling with projectile motion; the constraint here is the ladder's fixed length, not gravity, and the path is a circle.
2. **The full circle as the answer** — the *mathematical* locus is the circle; the *physical* trace is the quarter arc; a complete answer states both and distinguishes them.
3. **No endpoint check** — the rung starts at (0, L/2) and ends at (L/2, 0); the sketch without these anchors is incomplete.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: the circumcentre theorem</b>
</summary>

One classical fact ends the question: the midpoint of the hypotenuse of a right triangle is equidistant from all three vertices. The rung is that midpoint, the corner is one vertex, and the ladder's far end is always L away — so the rung stays exactly L/2 from the corner throughout: a circle of radius L/2, instantly, with the quarter-arc restriction read off the start and end positions.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: ellipses on the ladder</b>
</summary>

The same constraint gives every fixed point of the ladder an elliptical path — parametrise a point at fraction λ along the ladder as (λs, (1−λ)t) with s² + t² = L² and eliminate: X²/(λL)² + Y²/((1−λ)L)² = 1. The midpoint (λ = 1/2) is the special case where the two semi-axes coincide — the circle. The device is the trammel of Archimedes, two thousand years old and still the cleanest ellipse drawer.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b>
</summary>

A quarter circle of radius L/2 centred at the wall-floor corner. With foot (s, 0) and top (0, t): s² + t² = L²; the rung (s/2, t/2) satisfies X² + Y² = (L/2)². Instant proof via the midpoint-of-hypotenuse theorem: the rung stays exactly L/2 from the corner throughout the fall. Mathematical locus: the circle; physical trace: the quarter arc from (0, L/2) to (L/2, 0). Kinematics from a constraint — no forces needed.

</details>

#### Q72: Tiling a 2 × n Grid (T2-07)

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — the organising question is recursion</b>
</summary>

Cover everything below. Say first: n lives inside the question, so the question wants a recurrence — "how does a 2×n tiling relate to smaller boards?" Compute the first cases by hand, then find the argument that generates the rest.

> The official progression for this classic (compute, spot, name, generalise, vary) is the template for all such counting problems — the variations the examiner fires next are part of the design.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "How many ways are there to cover a 2 x n rectangular grid with 2 x 1 tiles?"</b>
</summary>

Follow-ups the examiner fires next (unquoted): what if 2×2 tiles are also allowed? What about a 3×n board with dominoes only?

Attempt it yourself before opening anything.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

- Look at the leftmost column: in how many distinct ways can tiles cover it? Each way leaves a smaller board.
- Why must horizontal tiles come in stacked pairs? What does a single horizontal leave behind?
- For the 3×n board: count squares — what does parity say before any other work?

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: Condition on the leftmost tile, case by case</b>
</summary>

*The core question.* f(n) = number of tilings of a 2×n board by 2×1 tiles (rotatable). Small cases: f(1) = 1 (one vertical), f(2) = 2 (two verticals, or two horizontals).

*Step 1 — condition on the leftmost coverage.* Option A: a vertical tile fills column 1 → remainder is a 2×(n−1) board → f(n−1) completions. Option B: horizontal tiles cover columns 1–2 — and a *single* horizontal leaves an unfillable notch, so horizontals come in stacked pairs → remainder is 2×(n−2) → f(n−2). These options are disjoint and exhaustive, so

f(n) = f(n−1) + f(n−2).

*Step 2 — generate the sequence.* f(1) = 1, f(2) = 2 → 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, … — the Fibonacci numbers shifted: f(n) = F(n+1).

*Step 3 — verify small cases.* Direct enumeration for n = 3: three tilings (three verticals; vertical + right-hand horizontals; left-hand horizontals + vertical) ✓.

*Follow-up 1 — 2×2 tiles added.* The left edge gains one more case: one 2×2 tile → g(n−2). So g(n) = g(n−1) + 2g(n−2), g(1) = 1, g(2) = 3 → 1, 3, 5, 11, 21, 43, … (closed form (2ⁿ⁺¹ + (−1)ⁿ)/3, roots 2 and −1).

*Follow-up 2 — the 3×n board.* Parity first: 3n squares, each domino covers 2 → **h(n) = 0 for odd n** — half the answer is free. For even n, single-variable conditioning fails (the left-edge configurations couple), and the correct tool is a coupled recurrence system; solving it yields the Pell numbers 1, 5, 29, 169, 985, … (characteristic root 1 + √2, the silver ratio).

Self-check: every recurrence is exhaustive by construction (the left-edge cases are disjoint and cover everything); small-case enumeration agrees at n = 2 and n = 3 for both f and g ✓.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — one move, three sequences</b>
</summary>

Every part reduces to one move: condition on the leftmost column. Two left-edge cases give the Fibonacci recurrence; one more case gives the g-recurrence; parity plus coupling gives the Pell sequence. The appearance of famous sequences is not coincidence but bookkeeping — recurrences are generated by choices, and different choice structures generate different signature sequences: φ for two cases, {2, −1} for three, 1 + √2 for the coupled system.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b>
</summary>

1. **Pattern-matching without proof** — listing 1, 2, 3, 5 earns nothing until the left-edge argument turns it into a theorem; the recurrence *is* the proof.
2. **Missing the notch argument** — a single horizontal tile leaves an unfillable cell; exhaustiveness requires noting that horizontals come in stacked pairs.
3. **3×n without parity, or with a single recurrence** — half the answer (all odd n give zero) is free, and the coupling genuinely requires a system; attempting a one-variable recurrence is the marker of an incomplete analysis.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: the left edge is the whole answer</b>
</summary>

Ask one question — "in how many ways can tiles cover the leftmost column?" — and the core collapses to two lines: f(n) = f(n−1) + f(n−2). The 2×2 variant appends one more term, and the 3×n board forces parity plus a coupled system. Recurrences come from choices, not from spotting patterns in tables.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: solving the recurrences</b>
</summary>

Linear recurrences solve via the characteristic equation: f(n) = f(n−1) + f(n−2) → x² = x + 1, roots (1 ± √5)/2, giving Binet's formula F_k = (φᵏ − ψᵏ)/√5 with φ = (1 + √5)/2, ψ = (1 − √5)/2 — so f(n) grows like φⁿ⁺¹/√5. g(n) = g(n−1) + 2g(n−2) → x² = x + 2, roots 2, −1. The 3×n coupled system has characteristic root 1 + √2. One technique, three famous constants.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b>
</summary>

Dominoes only: f(1) = 1, f(2) = 2, and conditioning on the leftmost coverage (one vertical → f(n−1); two stacked horizontals → f(n−2), since a lone horizontal leaves an unfillable notch) gives f(n) = f(n−1) + f(n−2), so f(n) = F(n+1): 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, … With 2×2 tiles added: g(n) = g(n−1) + 2g(n−2), g(1) = 1, g(2) = 3 → 1, 3, 5, 11, 21, 43, … The 3×n board: zero for odd n by parity; for even n a coupled recurrence yields the Pell numbers 1, 5, 29, 169, 985, … One move — condition on the leftmost column — drives all three counts, with characteristic roots φ, {2, −1}, and 1 + √2 respectively.

</details>

#### Q73: Verifying a Differential-Equation Solution (B-06)

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — verification is mechanical by design</b>
</summary>

Cover everything below. Say first: "show that X is a solution" questions are mechanical — differentiate twice, substitute, simplify to zero. And note the second layer this particular recollection carries: the statement itself is garbled ("No idea where n came from"), so part of the test is interrogating the question, not just answering it.

> A remembered statement containing acknowledged transcription errors is itself interview material: handling a flawed premise gracefully is a scored behaviour.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "Show that z_n = exp(-x\^2/2) is a solution to d\^2/dx\^2 (z_n) + x d/dx (z_n) + (n-1)x = 0. [something like that. No idea where n came from.]"</b>
</summary>

Attempt it yourself before opening anything.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

- Compute z′ from the chain rule — what factor does the exponent's derivative contribute?
- Differentiate again with the product rule, writing z″ in terms of z alone.
- Substitute into z″ + xz′ + z: watch every coefficient cancel.

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: Differentiate, substitute, simplify to zero</b>
</summary>

*Step 1 — first derivative.* z = e^(−x²/2); the exponent's derivative is −x, so z′ = −x·e^(−x²/2) = −xz.

*Step 2 — second derivative.* z″ = d/dx(−xz) = −z − xz′ = −z − x(−xz) = (x² − 1)z.

*Step 3 — substitute.* z″ + xz′ + z = (x² − 1)z + x(−xz) + z = (x² − 1 − x² + 1)z = 0·z = **0 for all x**. Verified identically — not at selected points.

*Step 4 — the garbled "n" (the transferable skill).* If the remembered term was "(n − 1)z" rather than "(n−1)x", the same substitution gives z″ + xz′ + (n−1)z = (x² − 1 − x² + n − 1)z = (n − 2)z, which vanishes iff **n = 2**. Recovering structure from a mis-remembered equation — by substituting and watching which coefficients must vanish — is exactly what the verification technique buys: the algebra itself audits the statement.

Self-check: the cancellation is exact for every x; the reconstructed family z″ + xz′ + (n−1)z = 0 has the unique exponent n = 2 ✓.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — the algebra audits the statement</b>
</summary>

Verification questions reward exact algebra and calm handling of flawed premises. The candidate's own flag ("something like that") is the correct instinct: substitute first, and let the coefficients tell you what the question must have been. That reconstruction move — interrogating a statement by substitution — transfers to every garbled problem you will ever meet.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b>
</summary>

1. **Sloppy differentiation** — z′ = −xz, not −2xz (chain rule on the exponent, which contributes a single factor −x); an arithmetic slip here turns a verification into a mess.
2. **Verifying at selected points only** — "for all x" means the identity must collapse symbolically; spot-checking x = 0 proves nothing.
3. **Ignoring the garbled term** — pretending "(n−1)x" makes sense forfeits the second mark; the reconstruction move (what must the term be for the claim to hold?) is the interview gold.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: let the coefficients vote</b>
</summary>

Substitute before interpreting: z″ + xz′ + (anything)·z collapses to (n − 2)z for a linear term, so the claim itself forces n = 2. One substitution both verifies the solution and repairs the question — in a garbled recollection, the algebra is the fact-checker.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: the full solution space</b>
</summary>

Reduction of order: with z₁ = e^(−x²/2) known, a second independent solution is z₂ = z₁∫ e^(x²/2) dx — not expressible in elementary functions (it is the Dawson function up to factors). The ODE is the Hermite/Gaussian-family equation; its polynomial solutions (the physicists' Hermite polynomials, for the right parameter) are the quantised harmonic oscillator's eigenfunctions — the "n" the candidate half-remembered.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b>
</summary>

z = e^(−x²/2) satisfies z″ + xz′ + z = 0 identically: z′ = −xz, z″ = (x² − 1)z, and substitution gives (x² − 1 − x² + 1)z = 0. If the garbled term was (n − 1)z, the same computation yields (n − 2)z = 0, forcing n = 2 — the substitution both verifies the solution and reconstructs the intended statement. Method: differentiate twice, substitute, simplify to zero; let the algebra audit the question.

</details>

#### Q74: Estimating √101 to Four Significant Figures (B-11)

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — anchor, expand, bound, cross-check</b>
</summary>

Cover everything below. Say the protocol aloud: anchor at the nearest perfect square, expand binomially with an explicit remainder bound, and let one Newton step serve as the independent cross-check. Four significant figures are safe *by construction*, not by hope.

> The candidate's retrospective on this interview — "I inexplicably decided arctan 1 = 1" — belongs to the adjacent graph questions, but the lesson generalises: in estimation, write the anchor explicitly before manipulating anything.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "Estimate sqrt(101) to 4sf"</b>
</summary>

Attempt it yourself before opening anything.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

- What is the nearest perfect square to 101? Write √101 as (that root) × √(1 + ε) — what is ε?
- The binomial series for (1 + ε)^(1/2) — how many terms do you need before the remainder is below the fourth significant figure?
- What is Newton's step for √N, and what does one iteration from your series value give?

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: Anchor, expand, bound, check</b>
</summary>

*Step 1 — anchor.* 101 = 100(1 + 0.01), so √101 = 10√(1 + 0.01): the anchor 10 is exact, the small parameter ε = 0.01.

*Step 2 — binomial expansion.* (1 + ε)^(1/2) = 1 + ε/2 − ε²/8 + ε³/16 − …: 1 + 0.005 − 0.0000125 + … = 1.0049875.

*Step 3 — multiply back.* √101 ≈ 10 × 1.0049875 = 10.049875 → to 4 s.f.: **10.05**.

*Step 4 — error control.* The neglected ε³ term is 10 × ε³/16 ≈ 6 × 10⁻⁸ — far below the 4th significant figure (0.0001), so truncation cannot affect the quoted precision.

*Step 5 — Newton cross-check.* x₁ = (x₀ + 101/x₀)/2 from x₀ = 10.05 gives 10.0498756… — identical to the series value. Two independent methods, one number: 10.0498756…

Self-check: 10.0498756² = 101.0000000 (to 7 s.f.) ✓; the remainder bound justifies the 4 s.f. claim rigorously ✓.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — safe by construction</b>
</summary>

Estimation is not guesswork: anchor exactly, expand systematically, bound the remainder explicitly, and cross-check with a second method. The quoted precision is certified by the bound, not by confidence. That certificate — "the neglected term is 6 × 10⁻⁸, so the fourth figure is safe" — is what separates an estimate from a hunch.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b>
</summary>

1. **No explicit anchor** — manipulating √101 directly instead of 10√(1.01) invites the "arctan 1 = 1" class of slip; writing the anchor is the guard.
2. **Truncating without a bound** — quoting 4 s.f. while the neglected terms could touch the fourth figure; the remainder estimate is part of the answer.
3. **One method only** — the Newton step takes ten seconds and catches any series slip; skipping the cross-check leaves the estimate unverified.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: two terms and a bound</b>
</summary>

The whole answer is 10 × (1 + 0.005 − 0.0000125) = 10.049875 → 10.05, with the ε³-term bound (≈ 6 × 10⁻⁸) certifying the fourth figure — and one Newton step confirming 10.0498756. Anchor, two terms, bound, check: four lines, fully rigorous.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: Taylor's theorem and Newton's quadratic convergence</b>
</summary>

The binomial series is Taylor's theorem about x = 100 in disguise; the Lagrange form of the remainder makes the ε³ bound a theorem rather than a plausibility. Newton's method for √N (the Babylonian iteration) converges quadratically — each correct digit doubles — which is why one step from a good anchor nails nine figures. Both are first-year university tools; the interview needs only their shadows.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b>
</summary>

√101 = 10√(1.01) ≈ 10(1 + 0.005 − 0.0000125) = 10.049875 → **10.05 (4 s.f.)**, with neglected-term bound ≈ 6 × 10⁻⁸ certifying the fourth figure. Newton cross-check from 10.05 gives 10.0498756…; squaring returns 101.0000000. More precisely: √101 = 10.04987562…

</details>

---

#### Q75: The Unit "Circles" of Other Norms (N-07)

<details>
<summary><b>🔍 Step 1: Opening — a reading-comprehension question first</b>
</summary>

Cover everything below. Say first: the word "magnitude" is quoted in the question — that is a warning that the familiar Euclidean meaning may not be intended. Before plotting anything, name what is actually being asked: all points whose distance-from-origin, under *some* sensible notion, equals 1.

> The source records three candidate routes for this question, and only the third scores: the first answers a question that was not asked, the second answers without a reason, the third derives. Watch yourself for the first two.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>💡 The interviewer: "Plot all points whose "magnitude" is 1, in 2D and in 3D."</b>
</summary>

Attempt it yourself before opening anything.

<details>
<summary>Stuck? Open this.</summary>

- If magnitude means |x| + |y| in 2D, split into quadrants: what does each quadrant's piece look like?
- In 3D with |x| + |y| + |z| = 1, what does one octant contribute?
- What familiar solid do the eight triangular pieces assemble into?

</details>
</details>

<details>
<summary><b>📐 Step 2: Clarify, split by sign, assemble</b>
</summary>

*Step 1 — pin down the meaning.* The quotes around "magnitude" invite a non-Euclidean reading; the natural candidate (and the one the interview intends) is the **taxicab norm** |x| + |y| (respectively |x| + |y| + |z| in 3D).

*Step 2 — 2D by case split.* In the first quadrant, |x| + |y| = 1 becomes the line segment x + y = 1 from (1, 0) to (0, 1). The other three quadrants give mirror images: (−x + y = 1, −x − y = 1, x − y = 1) — four segments assembling into a **diamond (a square rotated 45°) with vertices (±1, 0), (0, ±1)**.

*Step 3 — 3D by octants.* In each octant, |x| + |y| + |z| = 1 is a flat triangular face (e.g. x + y + z = 1 in the positive octant — the triangle through (1,0,0), (0,1,0), (0,0,1)). Eight such triangles assemble into a regular **octahedron** — the unit ball of the taxicab norm.

*Step 4 — state both layers.* The Euclidean unit "circle"/sphere are the honest answers if magnitude means √(x² + y²); the intended reading (and the richer answer) is the diamond and octahedron. A complete answer names the ambiguity, resolves it, and derives.

Self-check: the diamond's vertices are distance 1 from the origin in the taxicab norm ✓; the octahedron's faces lie at taxicab distance exactly 1 ✓; both shapes pass through the axis intercepts, as any unit ball must ✓.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎯 Step 3: Synthesis — the derivation is the answer</b>
</summary>

This is simultaneously a geometry question and a comprehension question. Route discipline: the Euclidean answer (circle, sphere) answers an unasked question; the memorised answer ("diamond, octahedron") answers without a reason; the scored route clarifies the ambiguity and derives by a sign case-split. The same discipline — resolve the reading before computing — governs every ambiguous interview question.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>⚠️ Trap check</b>
</summary>

1. **First-person Route 1:** "magnitude means length, so circle and sphere" — the Euclidean answer is premature; the quotes signal a non-standard reading, and answering the wrong question scores nothing.
2. **First-person Route 2:** "the answer is the diamond and octahedron" — the shape recalled from memory without a derivation is the same failure one level deeper; the examiner's follow-up ("why?") has no answer.
3. **A 3D sketch without structure** — the octahedron must be assembled from eight triangular faces; drawing "a diamond extruded" without the octant case-split is a guess, not a plot.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✨ A sharper route: case-split is the whole derivation</b>
</summary>

Route 3's core strike: one case split does everything. In 2D, four quadrants × one linear equation = four line segments = the diamond. In 3D, eight octants × one plane = eight triangles = the octahedron. The moment the sign cases are written, the shapes are forced — no memory required, and the "why" is built in.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>🎓 Beyond A-level: the family of norms</b>
</summary>

These shapes are the unit balls of the **ℓ₁ norm**; Euclidean is ℓ₂; and the third classical member, ℓ∞ (max(|x|, |y|)), gives the axis-aligned square in 2D and the cube in 3D. The pattern inverts in duality: the ℓ₁ ball in n dimensions is the cross-polytope, the ℓ∞ ball the cube, and they are polar duals — a glimpse of convex geometry that costs nothing to name.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>✅ Final answer</b>
</summary>

Reading "magnitude" as the taxicab norm |x| + |y| (resp. |x| + |y| + |z|): in 2D the sign case-split gives four line segments assembling into a **diamond — a square rotated 45° with vertices (±1, 0), (0, ±1)**; in 3D, eight octant triangles x + y + z = 1 etc. assemble into a regular **octahedron**. (If magnitude means Euclidean length, the answers are the ordinary circle and sphere — naming the ambiguity is part of the answer.) The derivation is one sign case-split; the memorised shape without it is the trap. (The full p-norm limit family — p → 0 and p → ∞, the square and the astroid — is this bank's superellipse question's territory; here the ℓ₁/ℓ∞ pair stands alone.)

</details>
